# CAFA Agent Example: My First CAFA Agent

## What is CAFA?

CAFA, pronounced /ˈkæpə/ (like 'Kappa'), is not a single tool but a comprehensive, multi-faceted initiative aimed at the digital transformation of intelligence. Its fundamental goal is to create a structured, participatory, and symbiotic relationship between human cognitive abilities and Artificial Intelligence.

The CAFA ecosystem is built upon five interconnected facets:

1. CAFA Ethos/Movement: This represents a fundamental shift encouraging individuals to transition from being mere AI users to becoming AI makers. It champions digital literacy and empowerment. A key initiative here is TEAM (Teacher Empowered Assessment Movement), which empowers educators to create custom AI tools.  
2. CAFA Framework: This is the theoretical backbone providing the guiding principles for how collective AI operates, emphasizing transparency, fairness, and human oversight.  
3. CAFA Platform: This is the practical, technological infrastructure designed for the creation, deployment, management, and iterative improvement of Generative AI Agents (known as CAFA Agents).  
4. CAFA Tokenomics: This is an economic model using token-based mechanisms to foster a sustainable, participatory ecosystem by rewarding contributions, funding projects, and enabling value exchange.  
5. CAFA Community: This is a diverse group including CAFA Agent Makers (Modelers) who create AI agents, End Users who utilize them, and CAFA Lab, Inc., which supports the initiative.

## What is CAFA Platform?

The CAFA Platform (https://ai.cafalab.com/) is the digital infrastructure that brings this vision to life. It is a comprehensive, low-code AI engineering platform for designing, developing, and managing generative AI agents.

### Key Features of the Platform:

* Hybrid AI Integration: The platform masterfully combines rule-based AI (for logic, structure, and predictability) with Large Language Model (LLM)-based generative AI (for creativity, analysis, and natural language understanding).  
* Modeler-Friendly Environment: It provides a low-code interface that makes AI development accessible to a broad range of creators, not just expert programmers.  
* Framework-Driven: The platform is built on proven prompt/context engineering frameworks like IMPACT (Iterative Multi-turn Process for AI Collaboration Technique) and emphasizes OMG (Ontology Model-centered Generation), which uses structured expert knowledge to enhance the validity and consistency of AI outputs.

This document will demonstrate how to use a specialized agent on the platform, the CAFA Agent Foundry Agent, to easily create your own powerful AI agents.

## Navigating the CAFA Platform to Build Agents

The CAFA Platform offers a user-friendly interface for building and managing your agents.

### Login Options

You can log in to the CAFA Platform (https://ai.cafalab.com/) in two ways:

* Option 1: With a CAFA Key (For Existing Users): If you already have a CAFA Key, enter your email and key to sign in. Remember to keep your CAFA Key confidential.  
* Option 2: With Google (For New and Returning Users): New users can sign in with their Google account. The system automatically registers you and you will receive a CAFA ID and Key via the email associated with your Google account.

### Register/Store LLM (e.g., OpenAI API) Key

To enable your CAFA agents to use Large Language Models, you need to register your personal API key (e.g., OpenAI API Key).

1. Get Your API Key: Visit https://platform.openai.com/api-keys to create a new secret key. You will also need to add a payment method for usage beyond the free tier.  
2. Store in CAFA Platform: Click on your profile picture (top right), go to "My Info," paste your API key in the "OpenAI Key" field, and click "Save."

### CAFA Training Account Policy

The use of the platform during and following the training period shall be strictly limited to purposes related to learning and exploring the CAFA platform. Due to the practical limitations and the economic burden involved in verifying whether such usage constitutes personal or institutional use, rather than use strictly for learning the CAFA platform, strict enforcement may not always be feasible — a situation that may result in regulatory forbearance. Nevertheless, any intentional misuse or abuse of this policy is strictly prohibited and may result in disciplinary or legal action. Individuals seeking to use the platform for purposes beyond educational or personal exploration of the CAFA platform are required to obtain an appropriate subscription, either under a personal or institutional account, as applicable.

## Methods for Creating CAFA Agents

On the CAFA platform, there are several ways to bring your agent idea to life, each suited for different needs and skill levels.

1. Build From Template: This is the easiest starting point. You select a pre-built agent and configure its parameters to fit your specific use case.  
2. Build From Scratch: For full control, you can create an agent from a blank slate. This can be done in two ways:  
   * Manual Coding: Write the agent's JSON code from scratch directly in the CAFA editor.  
   * Importing Code: Take complete CAFA agent code (e.g., from an instructor, training materials, or another agent) and paste it into the editor using the "Import from Text" feature.  
3. Build with the CAFA Agent Foundry Agent: This is an advanced and intuitive method where you don't write the code yourself. Instead, you interact with a specialized CAFA agent—the CAFA Agent Foundry Agent. The direct link to this agent will be provided by your instructor. You describe your agent's objective, framework, and logic in natural language (the "vibe"), and the Foundry Agent translates your description into the final, runnable JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) code.

This document serves as a tutorial for Method 3, showing how we use the Foundry Agent to generate the simple "Hello, World\!" agent described below.

## Agent Example Background

This example demonstrates how to leverage the "CAFA Agent Foundry Agent" to create the simplest possible CAFA agent: a single-turn translator. It takes user input and uses an LLM to translate it into Spanish. It serves as a true "Hello, World\!" for agent creation.

## How to Create This Agent Using "CAFA Agent Foundry Agent"

To create this agent using the "vibe coding" method, you would provide the following requests to the Foundry Agent:

1. Define Agent Objective: "Create a simple single-turn CAFA agent to translate user input to Spanish."  
2. Provide Agent Details:  
   * Title: Simple Spanish Translator  
   * Brief: A basic single-turn agent that translates text to Spanish.  
   * Description: This is a 'Hello, World\!' example for the CAFA platform, demonstrating a basic single-turn LLM interaction.  
   * Greeting Message: Hello\! Please provide any text and I will translate it into Spanish.  
3. Outline Content and Logic:  
   * System Prompt: "You are a helpful translation assistant. Translate the user's text into Spanish."  
   * User Prompt: "" (empty, to wait for user input)

By providing these details, the Foundry Agent generates the complete JSON code for the agent.

## Full Agent Code

{
    "options": {
        "title": "Simple Spanish Translator",
        "brief": "A basic single-turn agent that translates text to Spanish.",
        "name": "Simple Spanish Translator",
        "description": "This agent is a 'Hello, World!' example for the CAFA platform, demonstrating a basic single-turn LLM interaction.",
        "greeting": "Hello! Please provide any text and I will translate it into Spanish.",
        "params": {}
    },
    "prompts": [
        {
            "system": "You are a helpful translation assistant. Translate the user's text into Spanish.",
            "user": "",
            "temperature": "0.1",
            "max-tokens": "2000",
            "markdown": true,
            "show": true,
            "model": "gpt-4.1-nano"
        }
    ]
}

You can import the above code into the CAFA platform by following these steps:

1. Click the copy button located at the top-right of the code to copy the CAFA agent code.  
2. Go to ai.cafalab.com.  
3. Click 'Create Agent'.  
4. Select 'Build from Scratch'.  
5. Click 'Import from Text'.  
6. Paste the copied code into the text field.  
7. Click 'Import'.  
8. Click the 'Save' button. This saves the current state of the app you are working on, including all settings, prompts, and configurations. You will then see the assigned App/Agent ID.  
9. Click the 'Run' button next to the Agent ID to be taken to the agent's direct link.  
10. Click the 'Open' button to see the list of all Agents you have developed. You can save up to 10 agents with a training account.

## Detailed Code Explanation

A CAFA agent's code is a JSON object with two main parts: options and prompts. Let's break down what each part does in this simple example.

### 1\. The options Object: The Agent's Identity

This section defines the agent's metadata and configuration. It tells the CAFA platform how the agent should look and behave at a high level.

* "title": "Simple Spanish Translator": This is the main title the user sees. You may use HTML tags for formatting.  
* "brief": "...": A short, one-sentence summary of what the agent does. This is often shown when browsing a list of agents.  
* "name": "Simple Spanish Translator": The internal name for the agent.  
* "description": "...": A slightly more detailed explanation of the agent's purpose, which appears below the title.  
* "greeting": "...": This is the first message the user sees when they start the agent. It sets the context and provides an initial instruction.  
* "params": {}: This object is where you can pre-define Agent Parameters (variables). Our simple agent doesn't need any, so it's empty. More complex agents use this to store lists of questions, AI personas, or other data.

### 2\. The prompts Array: The Agent's Workflow

This is an array that defines the sequence of "turns" or steps the agent will take. Since this is a single-turn agent, our array has only one object inside it.

* "system": "You are a helpful translation assistant...": This is the system prompt. It's the core instruction for the Large Language Model (LLM), defining its role (a translator) and its task (translate to Spanish). This prompt is not directly visible to the user.  
* "user": "": This is the user prompt. When it's an empty string "", it tells the CAFA platform to pause and wait for the user to type something. The text the user enters is then sent to the LLM along with the system prompt. This is the key to creating an interactive experience.  
* "temperature": "0.1": This controls the LLM's creativity. A low value like 0.1 makes the output more focused and deterministic, which is ideal for a translation task.  
* "max-tokens": "2000": This sets the maximum length of the AI's response.  
* "markdown": true: This tells the platform to render the final output as Markdown, allowing for better formatting.  
* "show": true: This makes the output of the turn visible to the user.  
* "model": "gpt-4.1-nano": This specifies which LLM to use for the task.

## Mermaid Code for the Agent Execution Flow

graph TD  
    A\[Start: Agent Displays Greeting\] \--\> B{User provides text to translate};  
    B \--\> C\[LLM generates Spanish translation\];  
    C \--\> D(End Session);

## Best Practice and Key Takeaways

* The Core Interaction Loop: This single turn demonstrates the most fundamental concept in CAFA: a system prompt to instruct the AI and an empty user prompt to capture human input.  
* Simplicity is Key: For many tasks, a single, well-defined LLM turn is all you need. Don't overcomplicate the agent if a simple instruction can achieve the goal.  
* Separation of Concerns: Even in this simple agent, the options object (the agent's identity) is separate from the prompts array (the agent's logic). This is a foundational principle for building scalable agents.

## Possible Extensions

* Translate to Other Languages: Modify the system prompt to translate the text into other languages, such as Chinese or Korean.  
* Add a Persona: Modify the system prompt to give the translator a personality, such as "You are a friendly travel guide... Translate the user's text into Spanish and add a fun fact about a Spanish-speaking country."  
* Format the Output: Change the system prompt to request a specific format, like "Provide the translation in a table with the original text in the first column and the Spanish translation in the second."  
* Control the Tone: Adjust the system prompt to control the tone of the translation, for example, "Translate the user's text into formal Spanish" or "Translate this into casual, conversational Spanish."  
* Explore Advanced Features: This is just the beginning. The CAFA platform includes a wide range of commands, content operations, and design frameworks that allow for much more complex and powerful agent behaviors.

# CAFA Agent Example: Simple GAMER Workflow with System Parameter Deep Dive

## 1\. Background: Understanding Turns and Memory in CAFA

This agent demonstrates a foundational CAFA framework: GAMER (Generative AI Meta-learning and Evolutionary Reflection). GAMER is a three-step process (Draft, Critique, Refine) designed for tasks requiring iterative improvement, such as content creation or analysis. This specific example uses GAMER to help a user draft, critique, and refine a simple "Thank You" note.

More importantly, this agent serves as a detailed tutorial on two fundamental concepts in CAFA development: Turn Types (Symbolic vs. LLM) and System Parameters (specifically @TUt@, @TRt@, and @TSt@) which act as the agent's short-term memory.

### Thick Introduction: Symbolic Turn vs. LLM Turn

Every step an agent takes is called a turn, defined as an object within the prompts array. There are two distinct types:

1. Symbolic Turn ⚙️:  
   * What it is: A rule-based turn processed directly by the CAFA platform's internal logic engine. It bypasses the Large Language Model (LLM) entirely.  
   * How it's triggered: A turn becomes Symbolic if its user or system prompt string starts with a forward slash (/) or a control flow command (like @REPEAT()@, @JUMP()@).  
   * What it does: Executes predefined actions like setting variables (SET), performing calculations (EVAL), displaying UI controls (RADIO, TEXT), controlling the agent's flow (JUMP, REPEAT), saving/loading data (SAVE, LOAD), or simply displaying pre-written text (often including parameters).  
   * Why use it: For predictable, deterministic actions. It's fast, reliable, and essential for managing the agent's state, collecting structured input, and controlling the overall workflow. Think of it as the agent's internal "script" or "rules engine". In this example, Turn 4 is a Symbolic Turn used purely for explanation.  
2. LLM Turn 🤖:  
   * What it is: A dynamic turn where the agent sends information (system prompt, user prompt, context) to an external Large Language Model (like Gemini or GPT) to generate a new, context-aware response.  
   * How it's triggered: This is the default behavior. If a turn doesn't meet the criteria for a Symbolic Turn (doesn't start with / or a control command), it's treated as an LLM Turn.  
   * What it does: Generates creative text, analyzes information, answers questions, holds conversations, makes judgments based on provided context.  
   * Why use it: For tasks requiring natural language understanding, generation, creativity, analysis, or complex reasoning that goes beyond simple rules. Think of it as accessing the agent's "brain" for complex thought. In this example, Turns 1, 2, and 3 are LLM Turns, each performing a distinct step in the GAMER process (Draft, Critique, Refine).

### Thick Introduction: System Parameters @TUt@, @TRt@, @TSt@ (Agent Memory)

For an agent to perform multi-step tasks like GAMER, it needs memory. It needs to remember what happened in previous turns. System Parameters (SPs) provide this crucial short-term memory. The three most fundamental SPs for accessing past turn data are:

* @TUt@ (Turn 't' User Prompt):  
  * What it holds: Stores the exact content that was in the user prompt field of turn number t.  
  * When it's useful: Essential for recalling *what the user originally asked for* or *what specific input they provided* in a previous step. In our GAMER agent (Turn 2), @TU1@ is used to remind the "Critic" AI what the user's initial request was, so it can evaluate if the draft met those requirements.  
* @TRt@ (Turn 't' Result):  
  * What it holds: Stores the output generated by turn number t. If turn t was an LLM turn, @TRt@ holds the AI's generated response. If it was a Symbolic turn displaying content, it holds that displayed content.  
  * When it's useful: This is the most common way to chain turns together. The output (Result) of one turn becomes the input for the next. In our GAMER agent, @TR1@ (the initial draft) is fed into Turn 2 for critique, and both @TR1@ (draft) and @TR2@ (critique) are fed into Turn 3 for refinement.  
* @TSt@ (Turn 't' System Prompt):  
  * What it holds: Stores the exact content that was in the system prompt field of turn number t.  
  * When it's useful: Useful if you need to re-use the *same instructions* given to the AI in a previous turn, or if you need to analyze the instructions themselves. While less common than @TUt@ and @TRt@ for chaining results, it's available for complex scenarios. (This agent doesn't explicitly use @TSt@ for chaining, but it demonstrates its existence).

Dynamic Referencing with TN: While you *can* use absolute numbers (like @TR1@), it's best practice to use the TN command for relative referencing (like @TR@TN(-1)@@ for "the result of the previous turn"). This makes your agent more robust if you add or remove turns later. This example uses absolute numbers for clarity in explaining the specific parameters, but TN is generally recommended.

This agent will now walk you through the GAMER process, explicitly showing how these concepts work together.

## 2\. Full Agent Code

{
    "options": {
        "title": "Simple GAMER: Thank You Note Refiner",
        "name": "GAMER Simple Thank You Note",
        "brief": "Drafts, critiques, and refines a simple thank you note using the GAMER framework.",
        "description": "This agent demonstrates the 3-step GAMER process (Draft, Critique, Refine) and explains Symbolic vs LLM turns and the use of TR, TU system parameters for memory.",
        "greeting": "Let's write a thank you note! Who do you want to thank, and what for?",
        "params": {}
    },
    "prompts": [
        {
            "system": "You are a helpful assistant acting as a **Drafter**. Based on the user's request (who to thank and why), write a short, simple, and polite first draft of a thank you note (2-3 sentences).",
            "user": "",
            "temperature": "0.5",
            "max-tokens": "2000",
            "markdown": true,
            "show": true,
            "model": "gpt-4.1-nano"
        },
        {
            "system": "You are a constructive **Critic**. Your goal is to review the draft thank you note based on the user's original request. Check if it clearly states who is being thanked and why. Suggest one specific improvement for clarity or warmth. Provide only the critique.",
            "user": "- Original Request: @TU1@\n\n - Draft Note:\n@TR1@",
            "temperature": "0.1",
            "max-tokens": "2000",
            "markdown": true,
            "show": true,
            "model": "gpt-4.1-nano"
        },
        {
            "system": "You are a skilled **Refiner**. Integrate the critique provided below to revise the initial draft thank you note. Produce the final, improved version.",
            "user": "- Original Request: @TU1@\n\n - Draft Note:\n@TR1@\n\n - Critique (@TR2@):\n@TR2@",
            "temperature": "0.3",
            "max-tokens": "2000",
            "markdown": true,
            "show": true,
            "model": "gpt-4.1-nano"
        },
        {
            "system": "",
            "user": "/ **Explanation Turn (Symbolic Turn ⚙️)**\n\n**Process Complete! Let's Recap:**\n\n1.  **Turn 1 (Draft - LLM Turn 🤖):** You provided the initial request (`TU1`). The AI, acting as a Drafter, generated the first version (`TR1`).\n2.  **Turn 2 (Critique - LLM Turn 🤖):** The AI switched personas to a Critic. It received your original request (`TU1`) and the draft (`TR1`) as input and generated feedback (`TR2`). This demonstrates using **TU** and **TR** parameters to provide context.\n3.  **Turn 3 (Refine - LLM Turn 🤖):** The AI became a Refiner. It used the original request (`TU1`), the draft (`TR1`), *and* the critique (`TR2`) to create the final version you see above (`TR3`). This shows chaining multiple pieces of memory.\n4.  **Turn 4 (This Explanation - Symbolic Turn ⚙️):** This turn started with a `/`, so it bypassed the LLM. It simply displays this pre-written explanation, pulling in the values from previous turns using **TR** and **TU** parameters.",
            "markdown": true,
            "show": true,
            "model": null
        }
    ]
}

## 3\. Detailed Code Explanation

This agent follows the 3-step GAMER framework, with an added 4th turn for explanation.

* Turn 1: Draft (LLM Turn 🤖)  
  * system: Defines the AI's role as a Drafter.  
  * user: "": This makes it an LLM turn that pauses and waits for the user's initial input (who to thank and why).  
  * Memory: The user's input is automatically stored in @TU1@. The AI's generated draft note is stored in @TR1@.  
  * show: true: The drafted note is shown to the user.  
* Turn 2: Critique (LLM Turn 🤖)  
  * system: Changes the AI's persona to a Critic with specific instructions.  
  * user: This prompt *constructs the input* for the Critic AI. It explicitly includes:  
    * Original Request (@TU1@): @TU1@: Retrieves the user's initial request from Turn 1 using @TU1@.  
    * Draft Note (@TR1@):\\n@TR1@: Retrieves the AI's draft from Turn 1 using @TR1@.  
  * This is an LLM turn because the user prompt doesn't start with / or a command. It processes the context and generates a critique.  
  * Memory: The generated critique is stored in @TR2@.  
  * show: true: The critique is shown to the user.  
* Turn 3: Refine (LLM Turn 🤖)  
  * system: Sets the AI's persona to a Refiner.  
  * user: This prompt assembles all necessary information for the final refinement:  
    * Original Request (@TU1@): @TU1@  
    * Draft Note (@TR1@):\\n@TR1@  
    * Critique (@TR2@):\\n@TR2@: Retrieves the critique from Turn 2 using @TR2@.  
  * This is an LLM turn. The AI synthesizes the draft and the critique, guided by the original request, to produce the final version.  
  * Memory: The final refined note is stored in @TR3@.  
  * show: true: The final note is shown to the user.  
* Turn 4: Explanation (Symbolic Turn ⚙️)  
  * system: "": Empty system prompt.  
  * user: "/ \*\*Explanation Turn...\*\*": Starts with a /, making this a Symbolic Turn. The / itself acts as a comment anchor for the first line. The \\n allows the rest of the text to be displayed.  
  * Logic: This turn does not call the LLM. It simply displays the pre-written explanation.  
  * Memory Access: It demonstrates accessing memory from multiple previous turns (@TU1@, @TR1@, @TR2@, @TR3@) to construct the explanation text.  
  * model: null: Explicitly indicates no LLM is needed (good practice for Symbolic turns).  
  * show: true: The explanation is shown to the user.

## 4\. Mermaid Code for the Agent Execution Flow

graph TD  
    A\[Start: User provides request \- Who/Why\] \--\> B(T1: Draft Note \- LLM);  
    B \-- Draft (@TR1@) & Request (@TU1@) \--\> C(T2: Critique Draft \- LLM);  
    C \-- Critique (@TR2@), Draft (@TR1@), Request (@TU1@) \--\> D(T3: Refine Note \- LLM);  
    D \-- Final Note (@TR3@) & All History \--\> E(T4: Display Explanation \- Symbolic ⚙️);  
    E \--\> F(End);

    style B fill:\#CCFFCC  
    style C fill:\#FFFFCC  
    style D fill:\#CCFFCC  
    style E fill:\#f9f,stroke:\#333,stroke-width:2px

## 5\. Best Practice and Key Takeaways

* Frameworks Structure Workflows: GAMER provides a clear, reusable pattern for iterative tasks.  
* Turns Define Roles: Each turn can have a distinct purpose and AI persona, controlled by the system prompt.  
* System Parameters \= Memory: @TUt@ and @TRt@ are essential for passing information between turns, creating context and enabling complex, multi-step logic.  
* Symbolic vs. LLM: Use Symbolic turns for control, UI, and displaying fixed/parameterized text. Use LLM turns for generation, analysis, and understanding.  
* Context is Key: Providing relevant history (like the original request and previous drafts) in later turns (Turn 2 and Turn 3 user prompts) is crucial for the AI to perform its task effectively.  
* Explanatory Turns: Adding Symbolic turns that explain the process (like Turn 4\) can be very helpful for teaching users or debugging agent logic.

## 6\. Possible Extensions

* Add User Feedback Loop: After Turn 3, insert a Symbolic Turn asking the user if they are satisfied with the final note using a RADIO control. Use MAP and JUMP to either end the agent or loop back to Turn 3 (Refine) with additional user instructions.  
* Incorporate RISE: For more robust critique, replace Turn 2 with the RISE pattern: use REPEAT to run the critique turn 3 times (each with a slightly different critical lens defined in the prompt), then add an aggregation turn before Turn 3 to synthesize the multiple critiques.  
* Parameterize Personas: Define the system prompts for Drafter, Critic, and Refiner in the options.params object for easier modification and reuse.

# CAFA Agent Example: RISE Content Refiner with REPEAT Deep Dive

## 1\. Background: Iteration and Refinement in AI Agents

Many complex tasks require iteration – repeating a process multiple times to refine a result, gather different perspectives, or build upon previous steps. In CAFA, the REPEAT command is the primary tool for creating these essential loops.

This agent demonstrates the RISE (Real-time Intra-Self Evaluation) framework, an advanced pattern for content generation and refinement that heavily relies on iteration. RISE extends the basic 3-step GAMER (Draft, Critique, Refine) model into a 5-step process:

1. Generation: Create an initial draft of the content.  
2. Loop Setup: Use the REPEAT command to initiate an iterative critique phase.  
3. Repetitive Reflection: Run a critique turn *multiple times* (controlled by REPEAT), often asking the AI to adopt a different perspective or focus in each iteration.  
4. Aggregation: Synthesize the multiple, diverse critiques generated during the loop into a single, actionable summary.  
5. Evolution: Revise the initial draft based on the aggregated feedback to produce a final, more robust output.

The core idea is that multiple critiques from varied viewpoints lead to a more thorough and reliable refinement than a single critique pass. The REPEAT command is the engine that drives the crucial "Repetitive Reflection" stage.

### Thick Introduction: The REPEAT Command

The REPEAT command is a powerful control flow structure within the CAFA protocol used to execute a specific sequence of turns multiple times. It enables iterative workflows, essential for tasks like looping through data, generating multiple variations, or implementing frameworks like RISE.

Syntax and Parameters:

@REPEAT("turn\_start", "turn\_end", "number")@

| Parameter | Description | Constraints |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| turn\_start | The relative offset or absolute number of the first turn in the sequence to be repeated. Using TN for relative offsets is best practice. | Must refer to a turn *after* the current turn. |
| turn\_end | The relative offset or absolute number of the last turn in the sequence. | Must be greater than or equal to turn\_start. |
| number | The total number of times the sequence (from turn\_start to turn\_end) will be executed. Can be a number or an Agent Parameter (e.g., @PARAM\[N\]@). | Must be an integer of at least 1\. |

Example: @REPEAT(@TN(1)@, @TN(2)@, "5")@ placed in Turn 3 would execute the block of turns starting 1 turn after Turn 3 (i.e., Turn 4\) up to 2 turns after Turn 3 (i.e., Turn 5), repeating this block (Turns 4 and 5\) a total of 5 times.

Usage Rules:

1. Dedicated Symbolic Turn: The REPEAT command *must* be the only content within its own dedicated, hidden Symbolic Turn ("show": false). It cannot be combined with other commands or display text in the same turn.  
2. Double Quotes: All arguments (turn\_start, turn\_end, number) must be enclosed in double quotes ("). Single quotes (') are not permitted and will cause parsing errors.  
3. Forward Reference Only: turn\_start must always refer to a turn *after* the turn containing the REPEAT command. You cannot loop backwards.  
4. Symbolic Trigger: If @REPEAT(...)@ is placed at the very beginning of the user prompt (or is the only content), that turn automatically becomes a Symbolic Turn, bypassing the LLM.

System Parameters within REPEAT Loops:

When inside a block of turns controlled by REPEAT, special System Parameters become available, providing context about the loop's state:

* @R\_i@: The current iteration number (1-based index). This is extremely useful for processing items in a list (@MyList\[@R\_i@\]@), changing behavior on different loop passes, or labeling output (e.g., "Critique Iteration @R\_i@").  
* @R\_s@: The starting turn number (absolute) of the repeated block.  
* @R\_e@: The ending turn number (absolute) of the repeated block.  
* @R\_n@: The total number of repetitions specified for the loop.

Simple REPEAT Example (Non-RISE): Fun Fact Generator

This agent uses REPEAT to loop through a predefined list of topics (params.TOPICS) and generate a fun fact for each, illustrating the use of @R\_i@ and @PARAM\[N\]@.

{
    "options": {
        "title": "Fun Fact Generator",
        "brief": "Generates fun facts for a list of topics using a REPEAT loop.",
        "name": "Repeat with Pre-defined AP Example",
        "greeting": "I will generate fun facts about History, Science, and Art. Let's begin!",
        "params": {
            "TOPICS": { "org": "History|Science|Art", "cond": "SELF" }
        }
    },
    "prompts": [
        {
            "user": "/ Setup loop to run the next turn for each topic.\n@REPEAT(@TN(1)@, @TN(1)@, @TOPICS[N]@)@",
            "show": false
        },
        {
            "system": "Provide one single, concise fun fact about the given topic.",
            "user": "Topic: @TOPICS[@R_i@]@",
            "show": true,
            "model": "gpt-4.1-nano"
        },
        {
            "user": "/ Display all facts concatenated from the loop.\nHere are your fun facts:\n@TR@TN(-1)@@",
            "show": true
        }
    ]
}

*Explanation:*

* Turn 1 uses @REPEAT(@TN(1)@, @TN(1)@, @TOPICS\[N\]@)@. @TN(1)@ refers to Turn 2\. @TOPICS\[N\]@ gets the number of items in the TOPICS parameter (which is 3). So, it executes Turn 2 exactly 3 times.  
* Turn 2 runs 3 times. @R\_i@ becomes 1, then 2, then 3\. @TOPICS\[@R\_i@\]@ retrieves "History", then "Science", then "Art". The LLM generates a fact for each topic.  
* The results from all 3 runs of Turn 2 are automatically concatenated by the platform and stored in @TR2@.  
* Turn 3 displays the final concatenated results using @TR@TN(-1)@@ (which resolves to @TR2@).

Now, let's see how REPEAT powers the more complex RISE framework.

## 2\. Full Agent Code (RISE Content Refiner)

{
    "options": {
        "title": "RISE Content Refiner (REPEAT Example)",
        "name": "RISE Content Refiner with REPEAT",

            }

        },

        },

            "user": "RISE Step 5: Evolution\nBased on the aggregated recommendations, please provide the final revised version.\n\nInitial Draft (from Turn 1):\n@TR1@\n\nAggregated Recommendations (from Turn 4):\n@TR@TN(-1)@@",
            "show": true,
            "markdown": true,

            "temperature": "0.1"

## 3\. Detailed Code Explanation

This agent executes the 5 steps of the RISE framework sequentially.

* Turn 1: Generation (LLM Turn 🤖)  
  * RISE Step 1\.  
  * The agent acts as a Drafter. It waits (user: "") for the user's topic/request.  
  * It generates the initial draft based on the user's input.  
  * The draft is stored in @TR1@.  
* Turn 2: Loop Setup (Symbolic Turn ⚙️)  
  * RISE Step 2\.  
  * This is a hidden (show: false) Symbolic Turn dedicated solely to the REPEAT command.  
  * @REPEAT(@TN(1)@, @TN(1)@, @CRITIQUE\_LENSES\[N\]@)@: This instructs the system to execute the *next turn* (@TN(1)@, which is Turn 3\) exactly @CRITIQUE\_LENSES\[N\]@ (which is 3, based on the params) times. This setup drives the iterative critique phase.  
* Turn 3: Repetitive Reflection (LLM Turn 🤖 \- Inside the Loop)  
  * RISE Step 3\.  
  * This LLM Turn executes 3 times, controlled by Turn 2's REPEAT command.  
  * Persona: The AI acts as a Critic.  
  * Dynamic Prompting: The system and user prompts dynamically change with each iteration using @R\_i@ (the loop counter, value 1, 2, then 3\) and the CRITIQUE\_LENSES parameter from params:  
    * *Iteration 1 (@R\_i@ \= 1):* The AI is asked to critique the draft (@TR1@) focusing specifically on Clarity and Conciseness (@CRITIQUE\_LENSES\[1\]@).  
    * *Iteration 2 (@R\_i@ \= 2):* The AI critiques the *same draft* (@TR1@) but now focuses on Audience Appropriateness (@CRITIQUE\_LENSES\[2\]@).  
    * *Iteration 3 (@R\_i@ \= 3):* The AI critiques the *same draft* (@TR1@) focusing on Potential Counterarguments (@CRITIQUE\_LENSES\[3\]@).  
  * Memory: The results (critiques) from all 3 iterations are automatically concatenated together by the platform and stored in the System Parameter @TR3@.  
  * show: true: Each individual critique is shown to the user as it's generated, allowing them to see the different perspectives.  
* Turn 4: Aggregation (LLM Turn 🤖)  
  * RISE Step 4\.  
  * This LLM Turn executes *after* the REPEAT loop (Turn 3\) has finished all its iterations.  
  * Persona: The AI acts as a senior Editor.  
  * Input: The user prompt provides the concatenated critiques from the loop using @TR@TN(-1)@@ (which correctly resolves to @TR3@).  
  * Task: The AI synthesizes the multiple critiques into a single, organized summary of feedback and recommendations.  
  * Memory: The aggregated feedback is stored in @TR4@.  
* Turn 5: Evolution (LLM Turn 🤖)  
  * RISE Step 5\.  
  * This is the final LLM Turn.  
  * Persona: The AI acts as a master Refiner.  
  * Input: The user prompt provides the necessary context for the final revision:  
    * The initial draft from Turn 1 (@TR1@).  
    * The aggregated recommendations from Turn 4 (@TR@TN(-1)@@, which resolves to @TR4@).  
  * Task: The AI revises the original draft based on the synthesized feedback from the multiple critiques.  
  * Memory: The final, polished output is stored in @TR5@.

## 4\. Mermaid Code for the Agent Execution Flow

graph TD  
    A\[Start: User provides topic\] \--\> B(T1: Generate Initial Draft \- LLM);  
    B \--\> C{T2: Setup REPEAT Loop x3 \- Symbolic};  
    C \-- Loop Start \--\> D(T3: Iterative Critique @R\_i@ \- LLM);  
    D \-- repeats 3x \--\> D;  
    C \-- Loop Finish \--\> E(T4: Aggregate Critiques \- LLM);  
    E \-- Aggregated Feedback (@TR4@) & Initial Draft (@TR1@) \--\> F(T5: Evolve/Refine Draft \- LLM);  
    F \--\> G(End);

    style B fill:\#CCFFCC  
    style D fill:\#FFFFCC  
    style E fill:\#FFDDCC  
    style F fill:\#CCFFCC  
    style C fill:\#f9f,stroke:\#333,stroke-width:2px

## 5\. Best Practice and Key Takeaways

* REPEAT for Iteration: The REPEAT command is essential for automating multi-step reviews, generating variations, or processing lists. It's the core engine for iterative frameworks like RISE.  
* RISE for Robustness: Generating multiple critiques from different angles (Repetitive Reflection) and then synthesizing them (Aggregation) leads to more comprehensive, balanced, and reliable refinement than a single critique pass.  
* Dynamic Prompts in Loops: Using @R\_i@ within a loop allows you to dynamically change the AI's focus, instructions, or data source (like iterating through a list with @MyList\[@R\_i@\]@) on each pass.  
* Dedicated Control Turns: Keep REPEAT (and other control commands like JUMP, END) in their own dedicated, hidden symbolic turns. This improves code readability and prevents unexpected behavior.  
* Parameterize Loop Variables: Using an Agent Parameter (@CRITIQUE\_LENSES\[N\]@ or a dedicated NUM\_ITERATIONS parameter) to control the number of repetitions (number argument in REPEAT) makes the agent more flexible and easier to configure.  
* Concatenation Awareness: Remember that the results (@TRt@) from turns executed within a REPEAT loop are automatically concatenated into a single string. The Aggregation turn (Turn 4\) is specifically designed to handle this concatenated input.

## 6\. Possible Extensions

* User-Defined Lenses/Iterations: Add TEXTAREA or CHECKBOX turns before Turn 2 to allow the user to define their own CRITIQUE\_LENSES or specify the number of iterations for the REPEAT command.  
* Apply RISE to Scoring: Adapt this agent to implement the "RISE Workflow for Automated Essay Scoring" example. Turn 1 would generate an initial score, Turn 3 would iteratively critique the *scoring process* itself (checking for bias, rubric adherence, etc.), Turn 4 would aggregate feedback *on the scoring*, and Turn 5 would produce a final, refined score and justification.  
* Combine with INDEX/Ontology: If the critique lenses were part of a larger ontology model stored in params (e.g., LENS\_NAME | LENS\_DESCRIPTION | LENS\_EXAMPLES), you could use INDEX inside the loop (Turn 3\) to retrieve more detailed instructions or examples related to the specific @CRITIQUE\_LENSES\[@R\_i@\]@ for that iteration.

# CAFA Agent Example: Simple ASSISI Framework with Input Controls Deep Dive

## 1\. Background: Structuring Input for Intelligent Analysis

A core challenge in building interactive AI agents is bridging the gap between flexible human language and the structured data needed for reliable agent logic. How do you ensure the user's input is captured in a format the agent can understand and act upon consistently?

CAFA Input Control commands are the answer. These commands (RADIO, CHECKBOX, SELECT, TEXT, TEXTAREA) create interactive UI elements within your agent. More importantly, they symbolize human input – translating clicks and typed text into clean, predictable, machine-readable data strings.

This structured input is the foundation for robust agent behavior, enabling:

* Reliable Logic: Commands like MAP and EVAL can process the input predictably.  
* Targeted AI Analysis: LLM turns receive clearly labeled, unambiguous data, leading to more accurate results.  
* Controlled Workflows: Agents can reliably branch (JUMP) or loop (REPEAT) based on structured user choices.

This agent demonstrates these Input Controls within the ASSISI (AI-Supported Survey Instrument & Simultaneous Investigator) framework. ASSISI is a powerful two-phase pattern:

1. The Survey Instrument (Turns 1-7): A sequence of Symbolic Turns ⚙️ uses Input Controls to systematically collect diverse, structured data from the user. Each turn focuses on gathering one piece of information cleanly.  
2. The Simultaneous Investigator (Turn 8): A final LLM Turn 🤖 receives *all* the collected data simultaneously. The AI, acting as an expert analyst, synthesizes this complete dataset to provide a comprehensive, real-time summary, diagnosis, or report.

This example builds a simple "User Preferences Questionnaire" using ASSISI, showcasing each major Input Control.

### Thick Introduction: CAFA Input Control Commands

These commands are Symbolic – processed by the CAFA platform, not the LLM – and generate UI elements. Rule: Only ONE Input Control command is allowed per visible turn. Displaying a control pauses the agent and shows a "Submit" button.

1. RADIO Control (@RADIO()@)  
   * UI: Presents radio buttons (select only one).  
   * Syntax: @RADIO("name", "prompt", "options"\[, "other\_prompt"\])@  
   * name: Unique ID for this input (e.g., "color\_choice").  
   * prompt: Question text displayed (e.g., "Select your favorite color:").  
   * options: Pipe-separated choices (e.g., "Red|Green|Blue").  
   * other\_prompt (Optional): If present, adds a text box alongside the radio buttons. Used for SCREAM framework (capturing selection \+ explanation).  
   * Retrieval:  
     * Standard: @RADIO("color\_choice")@ returns the selected option (e.g., "Green").  
     * With other\_prompt: @RADIO("name")@ returns "SelectedOption|Written Text" (e.g., "Red|Because it is bright").  
2. CHECKBOX Control (@CHECKBOX()@)  
   * UI: Presents checkboxes (select multiple).  
   * Syntax: @CHECKBOX("name", "prompt", "options")@  
   * name: Unique ID (e.g., "topics").  
   * prompt: Question text (e.g., "Which topics interest you?").  
   * options: Pipe-separated choices (e.g., "Tech|Science|Art").  
   * Retrieval: @CHECKBOX("topics")@ returns a pipe-separated string of *all* selected options (e.g., "Tech|Art").  
3. SELECT Control (@SELECT()@)  
   * UI: Presents a dropdown menu (select only one).  
   * Syntax: @SELECT("name", "prompt", "options")@  
   * name: Unique ID (e.g., "country").  
   * prompt: Question text (e.g., "Select your country:").  
   * options: Pipe-separated choices (e.g., "USA|Canada|Mexico").  
   * Retrieval: @SELECT("country")@ returns the single selected option (e.g., "Canada").  
4. TEXT Control (@TEXT()@)  
   * UI: Presents a single-line text input field.  
   * Syntax: @TEXT("name", "prompt")@  
   * name: Unique ID (e.g., "user\_name").  
   * prompt: Question text (e.g., "Enter your username:").  
   * Retrieval: @TEXT("user\_name")@ returns the text entered by the user (e.g., "Alice").  
5. TEXTAREA Control (@TEXTAREA()@)  
   * UI: Presents a multi-line text box for longer input.  
   * Syntax: @TEXTAREA("name", "prompt")@  
   * name: Unique ID (e.g., "feedback").  
   * prompt: Question text (e.g., "Please provide detailed feedback:").  
   * Retrieval: @TEXTAREA("feedback")@ returns the full text entered (e.g., "The interface is good but...").

## 2\. Full Agent Code

## 3\. Detailed Code Explanation

This agent perfectly demonstrates the two phases of the ASSISI framework.

* Turn 1: Setup (Hidden Symbolic Turn ⚙️)  
  * Uses the SET command to define parameters (Q1 to Q6) that hold all configuration data (response name, prompt text, options) for each question. This centralizes content and keeps the subsequent turns clean.  
* Turns 2-7: The Survey Instrument (Visible Symbolic Turns ⚙️)  
  * This is the data collection phase of ASSISI.  
  * Each turn is a Symbolic Turn dedicated to displaying one Input Control.  
  * Turn 2 uses RADIO for single selection.  
  * Turn 3 uses CHECKBOX for multiple selections.  
  * Turn 4 uses SELECT for dropdown single selection.  
  * Turn 5 uses TEXT for short text input.  
  * Turn 6 uses TEXTAREA for long text input.  
  * Turn 7 uses the extended RADIO (with the 4th argument) to capture both a rating *and* a written explanation, storing them as "Rating|Explanation".  
  * The agent pauses at each of these turns, waits for the user's input via the UI element, stores it internally using the specified name (e.g., pref\_color, pref\_topics), and then proceeds sequentially to the next turn.  
* Turn 8: The Simultaneous Investigator (Visible LLM Turn 🤖)  
  * This is the analysis phase of ASSISI.  
  * It's an LLM Turn (no leading / in the user prompt).  
  * system: Loads the @ANALYST\_PERSONA@ to instruct the AI on its role and desired output format.  
  * user: This prompt meticulously constructs a complete report for the AI. It uses the input control retrieval commands (@RADIO(pref\_color)@, @CHECKBOX(pref\_topics)@, etc.) to gather *all* the structured data collected in Turns 2 through 7\. This entire data package is sent to the LLM in one go.  
  * The LLM receives the full context and generates the final analysis based on the complete set of user preferences.  
  * markdown: true: Ensures the AI's summary is nicely formatted.

## 4\. Mermaid Code for the Agent Execution Flow

    subgraph "Phase 1: Survey Instrument (Data Collection)"  
        A\[T1: Setup Questions SET\] \--\> B\[T2: Q1 RADIO\];  
        B \--\> C\[T3: Q2 CHECKBOX\];  
        C \--\> D\[T4: Q3 SELECT\];

        E \--\> F\[T6: Q5 TEXTAREA\];  
        F \--\> G\[T7: Q6 RADIO Ext.\];  
    end

    style A fill:\#f9f,stroke:\#333,stroke-width:2px  
    style H fill:\#bbf,stroke:\#333,stroke-width:2px

## 5\. Best Practice and Key Takeaways

* Structure Input with Controls: Input controls are essential for converting user actions into predictable data formats, enabling reliable downstream logic. Use the right control for the type of data needed (single choice, multiple choice, short text, long text).  
* ASSISI for Collect-Then-Analyze: The ASSISI pattern is highly effective when you need to gather multiple, distinct pieces of structured information before performing a holistic analysis, summary, or generation task based on the complete dataset.  
* One Control Per Visible Turn: Adhering to this rule ensures a clean user interface and predictable agent flow, as each control appropriately pauses the agent to wait for user input before proceeding.  
* Centralize Configuration: Using SET in an initial hidden turn (Turn 1\) to define all question parameters (names, prompts, options) makes the agent significantly easier to read, manage, and update later. Content changes are localized to one place.  
* Leverage Extended RADIO (SCREAM): The optional 4th argument in @RADIO() is powerful for capturing both quantitative (e.g., a rating) and qualitative (e.g., an explanation) data simultaneously in a single turn, streamlining data collection for frameworks like SCREAM.  
* Detailed Investigator Prompt: The final LLM turn (Turn 8\) succeeds because its user prompt meticulously labels and provides *all* collected data points. Giving the AI clear, well-structured context is crucial for accurate analysis.

## 6\. Possible Extensions

This foundational agent demonstrates the core ASSISI pattern and Input Controls. It can be extended in many ways to create more sophisticated applications:

1. Intermediate Scoring/Logic: Insert hidden Symbolic Turns between the input collection turns (e.g., after Turn 2 or Turn 4\) to perform immediate checks or calculations. Use MAP to compare a RADIO or SELECT response against a correct answer or predefined values, perhaps storing points in a USER\_SCORE parameter updated with EVAL.  
2. SCREAM Framework Integration: Fully implement the SCREAM (Selected and Constructed Response Evaluation by AI Model) framework. Use the extended RADIO control (Turn 7\) to capture both the Selected Response (rating) and Constructed Response (explanation). Then, enhance the final analysis turn (Turn 8\) or add a subsequent LLM turn specifically designed to compare the SR and CR, providing deeper diagnostic feedback based on the user's reasoning.  
3. Dynamic Routing Based on Analysis: Add a hidden Symbolic Turn 9 *after* the analysis (Turn 8). This turn could use MAP to search the AI's analysis (@TR8@) for specific keywords (e.g., "very dissatisfied," "critical issue," "positive feedback"). Based on the findings, use JUMP to direct the user to different follow-up sequences – perhaps offering immediate support, requesting more details, or simply thanking them.

# CAFA Agent Example: Agent Parameter with INDEX Command

## 1\. Background: Structuring Knowledge and Enabling Lookup

A fundamental aspect of building intelligent CAFA agents is managing knowledge. Agent Parameters (APs), defined within the options.params object or dynamically using the SET command, serve as the agent's memory and knowledge base. They allow you to store structured information – often referred to as an Ontology Model – directly within the agent's code.

The power of APs lies not just in storing data (like lists of terms, definitions, or questions) but also in controlling how that data behaves using the cond (condition) property. This allows for dynamic agent experiences like randomized quizzes, sorted lists, or linked datasets.

Once you have structured knowledge in parallel AP lists, you need a way to retrieve related information. If you know a specific term, how do you find its corresponding definition stored in a separate list? This is where the INDEX command becomes essential. It acts as a powerful lookup tool, finding the position (index) of a value in one list, which can then be used to retrieve data from the *same position* in linked, parallel lists.

This agent serves as a detailed tutorial on:

1. Defining Agent Parameters: Understanding the org, cond, and desc keys.  
2. Parameter Conditions (cond):  
   * SELF: Maintaining the original order of items.  
   * SHUFFLE: Randomizing the order for dynamic presentation.  
   * SORT: Sorting items in ascending order.  
   * DSORT: Sorting items in descending order.  
   * LINK(TargetParameter): Ensuring parallel lists maintain their relationship even after shuffling or sorting.  
3. The INDEX Command: How to use it to find the position of an item and retrieve linked data from parallel lists.

We will demonstrate these concepts using a simple "Dynamic Flashcard" agent that shuffles terms and ensures their definitions remain correctly linked.

## 2\. Intense Explanation: Agent Parameters (options.params)

Agent Parameters are defined as key-value pairs within the options.params object. Each parameter *itself* is an object containing specific keys that define its content and behavior.

Standard Format:

"params": {  
  "PARAMETER\_NAME": {  
    "org": "Value1|Value2|Value3",  
    "cond": "SELF | SHUFFLE | LINK(TargetParameter) | SORT | DSORT",  
    "desc": "An optional description for documentation."  
  },  
  "ANOTHER\_PARAM": { ... }  
}

Key Breakdown:

1. "PARAMETER\_NAME":  
   * The unique identifier you will use to access this parameter in your agent's logic (e.g., @PARAMETER\_NAME@, @PARAMETER\_NAME\[1\]@).  
   * Must be enclosed in double quotes.  
   * Can contain letters, numbers, and underscores.  
2. "org" (Origin):  
   * Required.  
   * Contains the actual data for the parameter.  
   * Values are stored as a single string.  
   * Multiple values must be separated by a pipe character (|). (e.g., "Apple|Banana|Cherry").  
   * Crucial Note: Avoid using pipes (|) or at-symbols (@) *within* your actual data values, as these are reserved characters for the CAFA protocol and can cause parsing errors.  
3. "cond" (Condition):  
   * Required for standard parameters holding simple values or lists.  
   * Determines how the values in the "org" string are ordered or linked during the agent's session.  
   * "SELF":  
     * This is the most basic condition.  
     * The order of values in the "org" string is preserved exactly as written.  
     * Use this when the sequence matters or when no dynamic ordering is needed.  
     * Example: If "org": "Step 1|Step 2|Step 3" and "cond": "SELF", then @MyParam\[1\]@ will *always* be "Step 1".  
   * "SHUFFLE":  
     * Randomizes the order of the values in the "org" string *at the beginning of each agent session*.  
     * The shuffled order remains consistent *throughout that single session*.  
     * Use this for creating dynamic quizzes, flashcards, or any scenario where presenting items in a random order is desired.  
     * Example: If "org": "A|B|C" and "cond": "SHUFFLE", the first time you run the agent, @MyParam\[1\]@ might be "B". If you run it again, @MyParam\[1\]@ might be "C" or "A".  
   * "SORT":  
     * Sorts the values in the "org" list in ascending order at the beginning of the session.  
     * Alphabetical sorting (A-Z, case-insensitive by default).  
     * Numerical sorting (0-9).  
     * Use this when you need to present items in a standard order.  
     * Example: If "org": "Cherry|Apple|Banana" and "cond": "SORT", the list becomes "Apple|Banana|Cherry". @MyParam\[1\]@ will be "Apple".  
   * "DSORT" (Descending Sort):  
     * Sorts the values in the "org" list in descending order at the beginning of the session.  
     * Reverse alphabetical sorting (Z-A).  
     * Reverse numerical sorting (9-0).  
     * Use this for rankings or prioritizing items (e.g., highest score first).  
     * Example: If "org": "7|3|9" and "cond": "DSORT", the list becomes "9|7|3". @MyParam\[1\]@ will be "9".  
   * "LINK(TargetParameter)":  
     * This is the most critical condition for building Ontology Models with parallel lists.  
     * It forces the values in *this* parameter's "org" list to be ordered or shuffled in the exact same order as the TargetParameter specified in the parentheses.  
     * The TargetParameter must itself have a condition that defines an order (e.g., "SHUFFLE", "SORT", "DSORT", or another "LINK(...)"). You cannot link to a "SELF" parameter *if* the linking parameter needs dynamic ordering derived from the target.  
     * Use this to maintain the relationship between corresponding items in parallel lists. If you shuffle or sort your list of TERMS, you *must* LINK your list of DEFINITIONS to TERMS to ensure the correct definition always matches the term.  
     * Example:  
       "SCORES": { "org": "85|92|78", "cond": "DSORT" },  
       "STUDENTS": { "org": "Alice|Bob|Charlie", "cond": "LINK(SCORES)" }

       If SCORES sorts descending to "92|85|78", then STUDENTS will automatically reorder to "Bob|Alice|Charlie", keeping the student linked to their score.  
4. "desc" (Description):  
   * Optional.  
   * A brief string describing the purpose of the parameter.  
   * Used purely for documentation and has no effect on the agent's execution.

## 3\. Intense Explanation: The INDEX Command

The INDEX command is a fundamental lookup function used to find the position of a specific value within a list (Agent Parameter or any pipe-separated string).

Syntax:

@INDEX("list", "value\_to\_find")@

| Argument | Description |
| :---- | :---- |
| "list" | The pipe-separated string (often an Agent Parameter like @MyList@) in which you want to search. |
| "value\_to\_find" | The exact string value whose position you want to locate within the "list". Case-sensitive. |

Return Value:

* Returns an integer representing the 1-based index (position) of the *first occurrence* of "value\_to\_find" within the "list".  
* If "value\_to\_find" is not found in the "list", the command returns 0.

Why it's Crucial for Ontology Models:

The INDEX command is the key that unlocks the power of parallel lists defined with LINK, SORT, or DSORT. The typical workflow is:

1. Have a primary list that determines the order (e.g., TERMS with cond: "SHUFFLE" or SCORES with cond: "DSORT").  
2. Have parallel lists linked to the primary one (e.g., DEFINITIONS with cond: "LINK(TERMS)" or STUDENTS with cond: "LINK(SCORES)").  
3. Obtain a specific value from one of the lists (e.g., user selects a TERM, or you know a STUDENT's name).  
4. Use @INDEX() to find the position of that known value within its *original* list (e.g., @INDEX("@TERMS@", "Function")@ returns 2 even after shuffling).  
5. Use that returned index (2) to retrieve the corresponding data from all *other* parallel lists (e.g., @DEFINITIONS\[2\]@, @STUDENTS\[2\]@).

This ensures that regardless of how the lists are ordered (SHUFFLE, SORT, DSORT), the relationships established by LINK are maintained, and you can always retrieve the correct corresponding information using the index found by INDEX.

## 4\. Full Agent Code (Dynamic Flashcard)

{
    "options": {
        "title": "Dynamic Flashcards: Parameters & Index",
        "name": "AP Conditions and INDEX Demo",
        "brief": "Demonstrates SELF, SHUFFLE, LINK conditions and the INDEX command.",
        "description": "This agent uses SHUFFLE for terms and LINK for definitions. It presents a term, asks for the definition via RADIO, uses INDEX to find the selected definition's position, and compares it to the term's position to check correctness.",
        "greeting": "Welcome to Dynamic Flashcards! Let's test your knowledge.",
        "params": {
            "TERMS": {
                "org": "Variable|Function|Loop",
                "cond": "SHUFFLE",
                "desc": "List of programming terms. SHUFFLE randomizes the order each session."
            },
            "DEFINITIONS": {
                "org": "A storage location with a name.|A block of code designed to perform a particular task.|A control flow statement for specifying iteration.",
                "cond": "LINK(TERMS)",
                "desc": "Corresponding definitions. LINK ensures this shuffles identically to TERMS."
            },
            "OPTIONS_ALL": {
                "org": "A storage location with a name.|A block of code designed to perform a particular task.|A control flow statement for specifying iteration.|A type of data structure.|A way to handle errors.",
                "cond": "SHUFFLE",
                "desc": "A larger pool of options including distractors, shuffled independently."
            },
            "FEEDBACK": {
                "org": "Correct!|Incorrect.",
                "cond": "SELF",
                "desc": "Feedback messages in a fixed order."
            }
        }
    },
    "prompts": [
        {
            "user": "/ T1: Display the first term from the SHUFFLED list.\nTerm: @TERMS[1]@",
            "show": true,
            "markdown": true
        },
        {
            "user": "/ T2: Prepare options. Mix correct definition (@DEFINITIONS[1]@) with distractors (@OPTIONS_ALL[1:3]@) and shuffle.\n@SET(Current_Options, \"@DEFINITIONS[1]@|@OPTIONS_ALL[1:3]@\", \"SHUFFLE\")@",
            "show": false
        },
        {
            "user": "/ T3: Present the shuffled options using RADIO.\n@RADIO(\"user_choice\", \"Select the best definition:\", \"@Current_Options@\")@",
            "show": true
        },
        {
            "user": "/ T4: Find index of CORRECT definition (always 1 relative to TERM[1] due to LINK) and USER'S CHOSEN definition.\n@SET(Correct_Definition_Index, \"1\")@\n@SET(User_Choice_Index, \"@INDEX(\"@DEFINITIONS@\", \"@RADIO(user_choice)@\")@\")@",
            "show": false
        },
        {
            "user": "/ T5: Compare indices to determine correctness and display feedback.\nFeedback: @FEEDBACK[@MAP(\"@EVAL(\"@Correct_Definition_Index@ == @User_Choice_Index@\")@\", \"true\", \"1|2\")@]@\n\n- Term: @TERMS[1]@\n- Correct Definition: @DEFINITIONS[1]@\n- Your Choice: @RADIO(user_choice)@",
            "show": true,
            "markdown": true
        }
    ]
}

## 5\. Detailed Code Explanation

* options.params:  
  * TERMS: Uses cond: "SHUFFLE". Randomizes order each session.  
  * DEFINITIONS: Uses cond: "LINK(TERMS)". Crucially ensures definitions shuffle identically to terms.  
  * OPTIONS\_ALL: Uses cond: "SHUFFLE". Pool of options including distractors, shuffled independently.  
  * FEEDBACK: Uses cond: "SELF". Fixed order for messages.  
* Turn 1: Display Term (Symbolic ⚙️)  
  * Displays the *first* term from the shuffled TERMS list (@TERMS\[1\]@).  
* Turn 2: Prepare Options (Hidden Symbolic ⚙️)  
  * This new hidden turn now *only* handles the logic of creating the options.  
  * @SET(Current\_Options, ...): Combines the correct definition (@DEFINITIONS\[1\]@) with distractors (@OPTIONS\_ALL\[1:3\]@) and applies a final "SHUFFLE" to randomize the order for presentation. The result is stored in Current\_Options.  
* Turn 3: Present Options (Visible Symbolic ⚙️)  
  * This new visible turn *only* displays the UI control.  
  * @RADIO(...): Uses the Current\_Options parameter prepared in the previous turn to display the choices. Pauses for user input.  
* Turn 4: Index Lookup (Hidden Symbolic ⚙️) \- (Formerly Turn 3\)  
  * Runs after the user makes a selection.  
  * @SET(Correct\_Definition\_Index, "1")@: Establishes that the correct definition relative to @TERMS\[1\]@ is at index 1 in the linked @DEFINITIONS@ list.  
  * @INDEX("@DEFINITIONS@", "@RADIO(user\_choice)@")@: Searches the *full shuffled @DEFINITIONS@ list* for the text the user selected and finds its 1-based index.  
  * @SET(User\_Choice\_Index, ...): Stores the index of the user's choice.  
* Turn 5: Compare Indices & Give Feedback (Symbolic ⚙️) \- (Formerly Turn 4\)  
  * Compares Correct\_Definition\_Index and User\_Choice\_Index using EVAL.  
  * Uses MAP to convert the true/false result into index 1 or 2\.  
  * Uses the resulting index (1 or 2\) to retrieve the correct message from @FEEDBACK\[...\]@.  
  * Displays the feedback along with the term, correct definition, and user's choice.

## 6\. Mermaid Code for the Agent Execution Flow

graph TD  
    A\[Start: Agent Loads & Shuffles/Sorts/Links Params\];  
    A \--\> B(T1: Display First Item from Primary List ⚙️);  
    B \--\> C(T2: Prepare Shuffled Options List using SET \- Hidden ⚙️);  
    C \--\> D(T3: Display Options using RADIO ⚙️);  
    D \-- User Selects Option \--\> E{T4: Find Index of User Choice using INDEX \- Hidden ⚙️};  
    E \-- Indices (Correct vs. User's Choice) \--\> F(T5: Compare Indices & Display Feedback using MAP/EVAL ⚙️);  
    F \--\> G(End);

    style A fill:\#f9f,stroke:\#333,stroke-width:2px  
    style C fill:\#FFFFCC  
    style E fill:\#FFFFCC

## 7\. Best Practice and Key Takeaways

* Ontology is Power: Structuring knowledge in params with parallel lists is fundamental.  
* cond Controls Behavior: SHUFFLE creates randomness, SORT/DSORT create order, SELF maintains order, and LINK preserves relationships across lists during these operations.  
* LINK is CRITICAL: When shuffling or sorting one list (e.g., terms, scores), always use LINK on parallel lists (e.g., definitions, student names) to maintain data integrity. This is the heart of reliable Tabular Ontology Models.  
* INDEX is the Key: Use INDEX to find the position (1-based) of a known value (often user input) within a list.  
* Index Enables Retrieval: Use the index returned by INDEX to retrieve corresponding data from all LINKed parallel lists, regardless of their current shuffled or sorted order.  
* Symbolic Logic: You can build complex logic (like checking answers, sorting leaderboards) using only symbolic commands (INDEX, EVAL, MAP, SORT/DSORT, LINK) without needing an LLM, making the agent faster, cheaper, and more deterministic.  
* Separate Concerns: Keep knowledge definition (params) separate from execution logic (prompts) for maintainability.  
* Single Action Per Turn: Separate complex operations like preparing data (SET) and displaying UI controls (RADIO) into distinct turns for clarity and reliability.

## 8\. Possible Extensions

1. Full Flashcard/Quiz Loop: Wrap the core logic (now Turns 1-5) in a REPEAT loop (@REPEAT(@TN(1)@, @TN(5)@, @TERMS\[N\]@)@) placed *before* Turn 1\. Adjust internal references like \[1\] to \[@R\_i@\]@ where appropriate (e.g., @TERMS\[@R\_i@\]@, @DEFINITIONS\[@R\_i@\]@). Aggregate results using SET inside the loop and display a summary after the loop finishes.  
2. Add Examples/Rationales: Create more parallel lists (e.g., EXAMPLES, RATIONALES) in params with cond: "LINK(TERMS)". Display this extra linked information in the feedback turn (Turn 5).  
3. Leaderboard Example: Create STUDENTS (SELF), SCORES (DSORT), RANK (LINK(SCORES) \- might need manual population based on sorted index). Display a sorted leaderboard using a REPEAT loop that iterates through @STUDENTS\[@R\_i@\]@ and @SCORES\[@R\_i@\]@.  
4. LLM Feedback Integration: Replace or supplement the symbolic check in Turn 5\. Instead, send the term (@TERMS\[1\]@ or @TERMS\[@R\_i@\]@ if in a loop), user's choice (@RADIO(user\_choice)@), and correct definition (@DEFINITIONS\[1\]@ or @DEFINITIONS\[@R\_i@\]@) to an LLM turn instructed to provide explanatory feedback.
