# CAFA Agent Example: AGILE \- Essential

## 1\. Background: The AGILE Framework

AGILE stands for Adaptive, Generative, and Iterative Learning Engine. It's a CAFA framework designed to create a "closed-loop" or "self-improving" system. Its primary goal is to build an agent that doesn't just administer a test but evolves with every user. It merges the content creation power of Generative AI, the efficiency of adaptive learning, and the analytical power of performance logging into a single, cohesive cycle.

This "Essential" version of the AGILE framework demonstrates two of the three core pillars: Adaptive delivery and Iterative self-improvement. (The Generative pillar, which involves creating questions on the fly, is a possible extension).

The framework is built on three core pillars:

### 1\. Generative Content Engine 🤖

This pillar answers the question: "Where do the questions come from?"  
Instead of relying on a static, pre-written item bank, the AGILE framework uses Generative AI to create its assessment content on demand. This can happen in two ways:

* Instance Generation: The AI generates fully-formed, unique questions (items) for a user's specific session.  
* Template Generation (AIG): Automatic Item Generation (AIG) is a method where the AI generates structured item templates based on a set of rules (an ontology). The agent can then permute features of this template (like numbers or topics) to create a virtually unlimited supply of new, varied questions.

Benefit: This solves the "item exposure" problem, where a test becomes less valid as users memorize the static questions.

### 2\. Adaptive Delivery Engine ⚙️

This pillar answers the question: "Which question does the user see next?"  
The agent delivers the generated content using an adaptive logic, tailoring the assessment's difficulty to the user's real-time performance.

* Item-Level (CAT): In Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT), after a user answers a single question, the agent grades it and selects the next question (either harder or easier) to quickly pinpoint the user's precise skill level.  
* Testlet-Level (MST): In Multi-Stage Testing (MST), the agent administers a small "testlet" (a bundle of 3-5 questions) at a medium difficulty. Based on the user's score on that entire block, it then selects a harder or easier testlet for the next stage.  
* GAMSA (AIG+Testlet for Learning): The Generative AI-based Multi-Stage Assessment (GAMSA) is the most advanced model, combining the concepts of AIG and MST to create a fully dynamic assessment experience. The agent generates entire "testlets" on demand. Based on the user's score on a testlet, it then generates a brand new, harder or easier testlet for the next stage. This creates a fully personalized learning where both the content and the path are generated in real-time.

Benefit: This makes the assessment highly efficient, personalized, and more engaging, as the user is always operating in their optimal challenge zone.

### 3\. Iterative "Self-Growing" Engine 📊

This pillar answers the question: "How does the system get smarter?"  
This is the most critical component for self-improvement. The AGILE framework implements a "between-task" iterative loop, where the agent learns from the cumulative data of all user sessions.

* Log Data: The agent saves the performance data from every session (e.g., which user got which item correct/incorrect) to its persistent LOG.  
* Import & Reflect: The next time a user starts a session, the agent begins by using IMPORT to load this complete history.  
* Evolve: The agent uses symbolic commands (EVAL, DSORT, LINK) to re-calculate its own internal parameters. Most importantly, it updates the difficulty (e.g., P-Index or P-Value) for every item in its bank. An item that many users get wrong will "iteratively" become "harder" in the system, and an item many get right will become "easier."  
* Export: At the end of the session, the agent uses EXPORT to save this new, evolved state back to the LOG, making it the baseline for the next user.

Benefit: The agent's understanding of its own content difficulty "self-grows" over time, making its adaptive logic more precise with every user.

### The AGILE Flywheel: Accelerating Learning

The true power of the AGILE framework is how these three pillars synergize to create a "flywheel effect" that accelerates learning.

The Iterative engine is the foundation. By constantly refining the item difficulty parameters based on real-world data, it ensures the agent's knowledge of its own content is highly accurate and relevant.

This accuracy directly feeds the Adaptive engine. Because the agent has a reliable difficulty value for each item, its adaptive selections become far more precise. It gets better at delivering the perfect question at the perfect time to keep the learner in their optimal challenge zone (or "zone of proximal development").

This, in turn, makes the Generative feedback cycle incredibly effective. When the agent provides adaptive feedback (like a hint from an AI Tutor), that feedback is now more accurate because the learning task itself is more accurate. The agent isn't giving a generic hint for a "medium" question; it's giving a highly specific hint for a question it knows has a P-Value of 0.65 for this user's peer group.

Consequently, the learner's journey is accelerated. They are not wasting time on items that are too easy or getting frustrated by items that are too hard. Every interaction is tailored, relevant, and supported by accurate, generative feedback, allowing them to build mastery more efficiently.

## 3\. Detailed Code Explanation

### The Ontology (options.params)

This section acts as the agent's knowledge base and initial configuration. It contains all the data the agent needs, separating content from the logic in the prompts array.

* Q\#\_DATA: Each parameter holds the content for one question: its stem, four choices, and the correct answer, all separated by pipes (|).  
* Item\_Names: This holds the names of the Q\#\_DATA parameters in their original order, which is crucial for updating the correct meta-data.  
* CATMAP: Defines the adaptive logic, mapping a relative rank to the next rank based on performance.  
* Total\_Exposure & Total\_Correct: These parallel lists store the performance data for each item. They are initialized to 0s to trigger the default logic if the LOG is empty.  
* DEFAULT\_EXPOSURE & DEFAULT\_CORRECT: These parameters hold the starting values to be used only on the agent's very first run.

### Turn-by-Turn Logic (prompts array)

The agent's workflow is a stable, sequential process broken into distinct phases.

* T1-T6 (Initialization & Sorting): This phase prepares the test.  
  * T1 (IMPORT): Loads the cumulative performance data from the persistent LOG.  
  * T2 (Conditional Defaults): A robust check using EVAL determines if the LOG was empty. If so, it applies the pre-configured default values. If not, it uses the loaded data.  
  * T3-T5 (Symbolic Sorting): These turns calculate the P-Index for each item, use DSORT to sort the values, and LINK to reorder the Item\_Names accordingly. This establishes the difficulty ranking for the current session.  
  * T6 (Initialize Session): Resets the USER\_SCORE and sets the starting item's relative rank (ITEM\_i) to 5\.  
* T7-T18 (The 4-Stage Adaptive Test): This is the core of the assessment, implemented as a stable, "unrolled" sequence of turns rather than an unreliable loop.  
  * Stage 1 (T7-T9): A 3-turn block that prepares the first question, asks it, and then grades the response, updates all meta-data, and uses the CATMAP to determine the relative rank for the next stage.  
  * Stages 2, 3, & 4 (T10-T18): This 3-turn block is repeated for the remaining stages, ensuring that the state (ITEM\_i, USER\_SCORE, etc.) is passed reliably from one stage to the next.  
* T19-T22 (Finalization & Reporting): This phase concludes the test.  
  * T19 (Placement): Displays the final score and the user's placement level.  
  * T20 (User Path): Shows a summary of the specific questions the user was administered.  
  * T21 (Bank Summary): Displays a full report of the item bank's status at the end of the session, including the newly calculated P-Indices.  
  * T22 (EXPORT): Saves the updated Total\_Exposure and Total\_Correct counts back to the LOG, completing the self-improving cycle.

## 5\. Best Practice and Key Takeaways

* Robustness Through Sequential Structure: This agent's final design proves that for complex, state-dependent loops, an "unrolled" sequential structure is the most reliable pattern in CAFA. By dedicating a block of turns to each stage, it completely avoids the race conditions and state management bugs that can occur with REPEAT or JUMP loops, guaranteeing a stable and predictable user experience.  
* The AGILE Flywheel in Action: The agent perfectly demonstrates the AGILE framework's iterative engine. The IMPORT (Reflection), symbolic sort (Evolution), and EXPORT (prepare for next Generation) cycle creates a self-improving system where the assessment's accuracy evolves with every user.  
* Configurable Defaults for Maintainability: Separating the initial "first-run" data into DEFAULT\_EXPOSURE and DEFAULT\_CORRECT parameters makes the agent much easier to manage. An administrator can change these baseline values without ever having to touch the complex logic in the prompts array.  
* Symbolic Power for Deterministic Logic: The agent's core intelligence—sorting, adapting, and updating data—is driven entirely by fast and reliable symbolic commands. This ensures its behavior is predictable and efficient, reserving the LLM for tasks that require true generation.  
* Dynamic Data Access (@@): The pattern of sorting a list of *names* (Sorted\_Item\_Names) and then using the @@ syntax to dynamically access the data associated with those names is a powerful technique for building flexible, data-driven agents.

## 6\. Possible Extensions

This foundational agent serves as a robust starting point. Its modular, ontology-driven design allows for several powerful and sophisticated extensions that can transform it into an even more dynamic and intelligent assessment tool.

* Generative Content (Full AGILE) using Validated Item Generation Templates: Instead of relying on a static, pre-written item bank, this extension implements the "Generative" pillar of the AGILE framework by generating content from pre-validated templates.  
  * Benefit: This approach offers a powerful balance between the consistency of a static bank and the scalability of pure generation. It ensures that while the specific questions are unique for each user, they still adhere to a known, high-quality structure.  
  * Implementation: The agent's ontology would be expanded to include 10 validated item templates (TEMPLATE\_1, TEMPLATE\_2, etc.). An initial REPEAT loop would be added (after T2). Inside the loop, an LLM turn would be given a detailed prompt containing the domain (e.g., "Algebra I") and one of the templates. The LLM's task would be to generate a single, concrete item instance from that template. The output would be parsed and dynamically SET as the Q\#\_DATA for the current session, building the item bank on the fly.  
* Generative Feedback (GAMSA Integration): This transforms the agent from a simple assessment tool into a personalized tutor.  
  * Benefit: Provides actionable, targeted feedback that enhances the learning experience.  
  * Implementation: A new, final LLM turn would be added after the score display (T19). The system prompt would define the AI's role as an "expert AI Tutor." The user prompt would provide the AI with all the data from the session, including the Your Test Path Summary from T20. The LLM would then generate a personalized feedback report, explaining concepts the user struggled with and suggesting next steps.  
* Advanced Error and Distractor Analysis: The current model only tracks whether an answer was correct or incorrect (1 or 0). A more advanced implementation would capture *which specific incorrect option* a user chose.  
  * Benefit: Provides much richer data for psychometric analysis, allowing you to understand *why* users are getting a question wrong and whether your distractors are effective.  
  * Implementation: The data saved to the LOG would be expanded. Instead of just a 1 or 0, you could log 1:CorrectAnswer or 0:SelectedDistractor. This requires expanding the EXPORT turn and building more sophisticated analysis tools, likely in an external system like Google Sheets, which could use COUNTIFS to calculate distractor efficiency.  
* Integration with Google Sheets for Longitudinal Tracking: While the agent's internal LOG is powerful for session-to-session improvement, long-term data analysis is best handled in a dedicated analytics tool.  
  * Benefit: Allows for the creation of dashboards, visualizations, and longitudinal tracking of both item and user performance over long periods.  
  * Implementation: The final summary report (T21) would include a tutorial section. It would provide the user with their unique Agent ID and LOG Pin and the exact \=ARRAYFORMULA(SPLIT(IMPORTDATA(...))) function to pull the raw performance data from the CAFA LOG directly into a Google Sheet for advanced, long-term analysis.

# CAFA Agent Example: AGILE 5-Stage Adaptive Test

## 1\. Background: The AGILE Framework

AGILE stands for Adaptive, Generative, and Iterative Learning Engine. It's an advanced assessment and learning framework designed to create a "closed-loop" or "self-improving" system. Its primary goal is to build an agent that doesn't just administer a test but evolves with every user. It merges the content creation power of Generative AI, the efficiency of adaptive testing, and the analytical power of performance logging into a single, cohesive cycle.

This agent is an upgraded version of the "AGILE \- Essential" agent, expanded to a 5-stage test using a 15-item bank to provide a more precise, 6-level final placement. It demonstrates two of the three core AGILE pillars: Adaptive delivery and Iterative self-improvement.

### The AGILE Pillars in this Agent

#### 1\. Adaptive (The Delivery Engine) ⚙️

This pillar answers the question: "Which question does the user see next?" This agent uses two layers of adaptation:

* Macro-Adaptation (Between Sessions): Before the test begins, the agent re-ranks its entire 15-item bank from easiest to hardest based on the cumulative performance data from all previous users.  
* Micro-Adaptation (CAT): During the test, it uses Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT) logic. After a user answers a question, the agent selects the next question (either harder or easier) from the newly sorted bank to quickly pinpoint the user's precise skill level.

#### 2\. Iterative (The "Self-Growing" Engine) 📊

This pillar answers the question: "How does the system get smarter?" This agent implements a "between-task" iterative loop:

* Log Data: It saves the performance data from every session to its persistent LOG.  
* Import & Reflect: The next time a user starts, the agent begins by using IMPORT to load this complete history.  
* Evolve: It uses symbolic commands (EVAL, DSORT, LINK) to re-calculate the difficulty (P-Index) for every item in its bank. An item many users get wrong will "iteratively" become "harder" in the system.  
* Export: At the end of the session, it uses EXPORT to save this new, evolved state back to the LOG, making it the baseline for the next user.

### The AGILE Flywheel: Accelerating Learning

The true power of the AGILE framework is how these pillars synergize to create a "flywheel effect." The Iterative engine constantly refines item difficulty, which makes the Adaptive engine's selections more precise. This ensures the user is always in their optimal challenge zone, accelerating their learning journey.

## 3\. Detailed Code Explanation

### The Ontology (options.params)

This section acts as the agent's knowledge base and initial configuration. It contains all the data the agent needs to run, separating content from the logic in the prompts array.

* Q\#\_DATA: Each parameter holds the content for one question: its stem, four choices, and the correct answer, all separated by pipes (|).  
* Item\_Names: This holds the names of the Q\#\_DATA parameters in their original order, which is crucial for updating the correct meta-data.  
* CATMAP: Defines the adaptive logic, mapping a relative rank to the next rank based on performance.  
* Total\_Exposure & Total\_Correct: These parallel lists store the performance data for each item. They are initialized to 0s to trigger the default logic if the LOG is empty.  
* DEFAULT\_EXPOSURE & DEFAULT\_CORRECT: These parameters hold the starting values to be used only on the agent's very first run.

### Turn-by-Turn Logic (prompts array)

The agent's workflow is a stable, sequential process broken into distinct phases.

* T1-T6 (Initialization & Sorting): This phase prepares the test.  
  * T1 (IMPORT): Loads the cumulative performance data from the persistent LOG.  
  * T2 (Conditional Defaults): A robust check using EVAL determines if the LOG was empty. If so, it applies the pre-configured default values. If not, it uses the loaded data.  
  * T3-T5 (Symbolic Sorting): These turns calculate the P-Index for each item, use DSORT to sort the values, and LINK to reorder the Item\_Names accordingly. This establishes the difficulty ranking for the current session.  
  * T6 (Initialize Session): Resets the USER\_SCORE and sets the starting item's relative rank (ITEM\_i) to 8\.  
* T7-T21 (The 5-Stage Adaptive Test): This is the core of the assessment, implemented as a stable, "unrolled" sequence of turns rather than an unreliable loop.  
  * Stage 1 (T7-T9): A 3-turn block that prepares the first question, asks it, and then grades the response, updates all meta-data, and uses the CATMAP to determine the relative rank for the next stage.  
  * Stages 2, 3, 4, & 5 (T10-T21): This 3-turn block is repeated for the remaining stages, ensuring that the state (ITEM\_i, USER\_SCORE, etc.) is passed reliably from one stage to the next.  
* T22-T25 (Finalization & Reporting): This phase concludes the test.  
  * T22 (Placement): Displays the final score and the user's placement level.  
  * T23 (User Path): Shows a summary of the specific questions the user was administered.  
  * T24 (Bank Summary): Displays a full report of the item bank's status at the end of the session, including the newly calculated P-Indices.  
  * T25 (EXPORT): Saves the updated Total\_Exposure and Total\_Correct counts back to the LOG, completing the self-improving cycle.

## 4\. Mermaid Code for the Agent Execution Flow

graph TD  
    subgraph "Phase 1: Initialization & Sorting"  
        A(Start) \--\> B\["T1: IMPORT from LOG"\];  
        B \--\> C\["T2: Apply Defaults if LOG Empty"\];  
        C \--\> D\["T3-T5: Calculate P-Index & Sort Item Bank"\];  
        D \--\> E\["T6: Initialize Session Variables"\];  
    end

    subgraph "Phase 2: Adaptive Test (Sequential Stages)"  
        E \--\> F\["T7-T9: Administer & Process Stage 1"\];  
        F \--\> G\["T10-T12: Administer & Process Stage 2"\];  
        G \--\> H\["T13-T15: Administer & Process Stage 3"\];  
        H \--\> I\["T16-T18: Administer & Process Stage 4"\];  
        I \--\> J\["T19-T21: Administer & Process Stage 5"\];  
    end

    subgraph "Phase 3: Finalization & Save State"

        K \--\> L\["T25: EXPORT to LOG"\];  
        L \--\> M(End);  
    end

## 5\. Best Practice and Key Takeaways

* Robustness Through Sequential Structure: This agent's design proves that for complex, state-dependent loops, an "unrolled" sequential structure is the most reliable pattern in CAFA. By dedicating a block of turns to each stage, it completely avoids race conditions, guaranteeing a stable and predictable user experience.  
* The AGILE Flywheel in Action: The agent perfectly demonstrates the AGILE framework's iterative engine. The IMPORT (Reflection), symbolic sort (Evolution), and EXPORT cycle creates a self-improving system where the assessment's accuracy evolves with every user.  
* Configurable Defaults for Maintainability: Separating the "first-run" data into DEFAULT\_EXPOSURE and DEFAULT\_CORRECT parameters makes the agent easier to manage. An administrator can change these baseline values without touching the complex logic.  
* Symbolic Power for Deterministic Logic: The agent's core intelligence—sorting, adapting, and updating data—is driven entirely by fast and reliable symbolic commands. This ensures its behavior is predictable and efficient.  
* Dynamic Data Access (@@): The pattern of sorting a list of *names* (Sorted\_Item\_Names) and then using the @@ syntax to dynamically access the data is a powerful technique for building flexible agents.

## 6\. Possible Extensions

This foundational agent serves as a robust starting point for creating even more sophisticated assessment systems.

* Generative Content (Full AGILE) using Validated Item Generation Templates: Instead of a static item bank, an initial LLM turn could generate 15 unique items based on pre-validated templates, creating a new test for every session.  
* Generative Feedback (GAMSA Integration): A final LLM turn could be added to act as an "AI Tutor," providing a personalized, narrative feedback report based on the user's test path and performance.  
* Advanced Error and Distractor Analysis: The data saved to the LOG could be expanded to include *which specific incorrect option* a user chose, providing richer data for psychometric analysis and item improvement.  
* Integration with Google Sheets for Longitudinal Tracking: The final summary report could include a tutorial on how to connect a Google Sheet to the agent's LOG, allowing for long-term data analysis and visualization of item performance trends.

# CAFA Agent Example: Basic REPAIR (Reverse Engineering Passage-based Assessment by Intelligent Reconstructor) for Listening

## 1\. Background

This agent demonstrates how to create a dynamic listening assessment within the CAFA framework, leveraging a Large Language Model (LLM) both for content generation based on user input (outputting directly to a pipe-separated format) and for grading free-text responses. It combines several key features:

* Topic-Based Generation: It leverages an LLM to generate relevant content (a reading passage, questions, and answers) based on a user-provided topic, directly outputting it as a single pipe-separated string.  
* Symbolic Parsing: A symbolic turn uses index access (@PARAM\[index\]@) to parse the pipe-separated string from the LLM, extracting the passage, questions, and answers.  
* Text-to-Speech (TTS): Provides an auditory component by allowing the user to listen to the passage via a TTS button.  
* Free-Text Input: Uses TEXTAREA to collect user answers, allowing for more open-ended responses.  
* Iterative Assessment: Administers the questions using a REPEAT loop.  
* AI-Powered Grading (Context-Aware): A dedicated LLM turn within the loop evaluates the user's free-text answer against the correct answer using the original passage for context. Structured output (output-values) ensures the grading itself remains reliable.  
* Auditory Results (Narrative): It concludes by using an LLM to generate a narrative summary of the results, including explanations based on correct answers, and reads this summary aloud using the automatic playback feature of the TTS command.

This agent showcases a pattern where one LLM generates structured content based on prompt instructions (aiming for pipe separation), symbolic turns parse this structure and manage flow, another LLM handles nuanced grading, and a final LLM generates personalized feedback. Note: The initial content generation (Turn 2\) relies heavily on the LLM perfectly adhering to the requested pipe-separated format.

This example draws its inspiration from the REPAIR (Reverse Engineering Passage-based Assessment by Intelligent Reconstructor) framework. REPAIR is a sophisticated methodology focused on generating reading passage-based assessments by systematically manipulating various features and contextual elements. For instance, the framework might take an existing reading passage and "reverse engineer" it to produce new questions, or it could generate entirely new passages and question sets based on specific inputs like target topics, desired difficulty levels, or specific linguistic features. The core idea is to automate the creation of diverse assessment materials by controlling the underlying attributes of the content. This particular agent represents a simplified and foundational application of the REPAIR principles, focusing specifically on the pathway of generating a unique passage and its associated question set directly from a user-provided topic, thereby demonstrating a core capability of the broader framework.

## 3\. Detailed Code Explanation

This CAFA agent implements a dynamic listening assessment. It generates content as a pipe-separated string based on user input, uses symbolic turns to parse and manage the data, employs an LLM for context-aware grading of free-text answers, and uses another LLM to generate narrative feedback which is then read aloud using TTS.

### 3.1. The options Object

* title, brief, name, description, greeting: Define the agent's identity and initial user message. Updated to reflect the narrative TTS summary feature.  
* params: Contains the configuration and prompts for the agent.  
  * GENERATOR\_PERSONA\_PIPE: Instructs the first LLM (Turn 2\) on its role and the required pipe-separated output format (Passage|Q1|A1|Q2|A2|Q3|A3).  
  * GRADER\_PERSONA: Instructs the grading LLM (Turn 8\) to compare the user's answer to the correct answer within the context of the passage, outputting only "Correct" or "Incorrect".  
  * SUMMARY\_PERSONA: New Parameter. Instructs the final LLM (Turn 11\) to act as an AI Tutor and generate a conversational, narrative summary based on the overall score and individual question results, including mentioning correct answers for incorrect attempts.  
  * TTS\_VOICE: Specifies the voice (nova) to be used for Text-to-Speech commands.

### 3.2. The prompts Array (Turn-by-Turn Logic)

* Turn 1 (Get Topic \- Symbolic): Uses the @TEXT() command to collect the desired topic from the user. Stores input under the name user\_topic\_context.  
* Turn 2 (Generate Content \- LLM \- Hidden):  
  * Activates the GENERATOR\_PERSONA\_PIPE.  
  * Sends the user\_topic\_context to the LLM.  
  * The LLM attempts to generate the passage, three questions, and three answers as a single pipe-separated string according to the persona's strict format instructions. The raw result is stored in @TR2@. No output-values constraint is used, relying solely on the prompt for formatting.  
* Turn 3 (Capture Raw String \- Symbolic \- Hidden):  
  * Uses @SET(RAW\_CONTENT, "@TR@TN(-1)@@")@ to capture the raw output from Turn 2\. This separation respects the dependency rule.  
* Turn 4 (Parse Pipe String \- Symbolic \- Hidden):  
  * Uses @SET()@ and index access (@RAW\_CONTENT\[index\]@) to parse the string captured in Turn 3\.  
  * PASSAGE: Extracts the first part (index 1).  
  * QUESTIONS: Combines the text from indices 2, 4, and 6 into a pipe-separated list.  
  * ANSWERS: Combines the text from indices 3, 5, and 7 into a parallel pipe-separated list.  
  * USER\_SCORE: Initializes the score to 0\.  
  * Crucial Dependency: This turn's success depends entirely on Turn 2 generating exactly 7 pipe-separated parts in the correct order.  
* Turn 5 (Display Passage & TTS Button \- Symbolic \- Visible):  
  * Displays the extracted PASSAGE text to the user.  
  * Uses the @TTS()@ command (@TTS("@PASSAGE@", "Listen to Passage", "@TTS\_VOICE@")@) to create a button allowing the user to listen to the passage.  
* Turn 6 (Setup Quiz Loop \- Symbolic \- Hidden):  
  * Uses @REPEAT(@TN(1)@, @TN(3)@, 3)@ to initiate a loop that will execute the next three turns (T7, T8, T9) exactly three times, once for each question.  
* Turns 7-9 (The Quiz Loop): This block executes three times. The system parameter @R\_i@ represents the current iteration number (1, 2, or 3).  
  * Turn 7 (Ask Question \- Symbolic \- Visible): Uses @TEXTAREA("ans\_@R\_i@", ...)@ to display the current question (@QUESTIONS\[@R\_i@\]@) and provide a multi-line input field for the user's free-text answer.  
  * Turn 8 (Grade Answer \- LLM \- Hidden):  
    * Activates the GRADER\_PERSONA.  
    * Provides the LLM with the full context: the PASSAGE, the current QUESTION, the CORRECT ANSWER, and the USER ANSWER (@TEXTAREA(ans\_@R\_i@)@).  
    * Uses output-values: "Correct|Incorrect" to constrain the LLM's output to only one of these two words, ensuring a reliable grading result stored in @TR8\[@R\_i@\]@.  
  * Turn 9 (Process Grade & Update Score \- Symbolic \- Hidden):  
    * Captures the grading result ("Correct" or "Incorrect") into RESULT\_TEXT\_@R\_i@.  
    * Uses @MAP()@ to convert the text result into a numerical score (1 or 0\) stored in RESULT\_@R\_i@.  
    * Uses @EVAL()@ to add this score to the cumulative USER\_SCORE.  
* Turn 10 (Display Results Summary \- Symbolic \- Visible):  
  * Executes after the REPEAT loop finishes.  
  * Displays a formatted summary showing each question, the user's answer, the grading result (@RESULT\_TEXT\_1@, etc.), the correct answer, and the final USER\_SCORE.  
  * Includes a note indicating that an audio summary will play automatically.  
* Turn 11 (Generate Narrative Summary \- LLM \- Hidden): Modified Turn.  
  * Activates the SUMMARY\_PERSONA.  
  * The user prompt provides the LLM with all necessary data: the final score, and for each question, the text, user's answer, correct answer, and result ("Correct"/"Incorrect").  
  * The LLM synthesizes this information into a conversational, narrative summary suitable for audio playback. The result is stored in @TR11@.  
* Turn 12 (Read Narrative Score Aloud \- Symbolic \- Hidden): Modified Turn.  
  * Uses the @TTS()@ command.  
  * The content argument is @TR@TN(-1)@@, which pulls the narrative summary generated by the LLM in the previous turn.  
  * The caption argument is "" (empty string). This instructs the agent to play the audio automatically as soon as the turn loads, without displaying a button.  
  * Uses the predefined @TTS\_VOICE@.

## 5\. Best Practices and Key Takeaways

* Dependency Rule Adherence: Separating data capture (T3) from parsing (T4) follows the dependency rule, improving robustness.  
* Direct Generation to Structure: Instructing the LLM (T2) to generate directly into a simple, parsable format (pipe-separated) can work but carries risks if the LLM deviates.  
* Symbolic Parsing: Relying on symbolic index access (T4) is efficient if the LLM adheres perfectly to the format requested in T2.  
* Increased Fragility: The symbolic parsing in T4 is the most fragile part of this agent. Strict prompt engineering in GENERATOR\_PERSONA\_PIPE is crucial.  
* Contextual Grading: LLM grading (T8) benefits from passage context and the reliability of output-values for its binary output ("Correct"/"Incorrect").  
* Narrative Feedback: Using an LLM (T11) to generate the final summary allows for more natural, conversational, and informative feedback, especially valuable when delivered via TTS.

## 6\. Possible Extensions

* Error Handling: Add checks after Turn 2 (e.g., using EVAL to count pipes in @TR2@) to validate the format before symbolic parsing in Turn 4\. If invalid, jump to an error message or retry generation.  
* Adaptive Difficulty: Modify the logic to select the next question's difficulty based on the previous answer.  
* SCREAM Framework: Modify Turn 7 to use @RADIO()@ with the 4th argument to capture both a selected response and a constructed response (explanation). Update the grading and summary turns accordingly.  
* More Detailed Narrative Feedback: Enhance the SUMMARY\_PERSONA (Turn 11\) to provide even more specific feedback or suggest learning resources based on incorrect answers.

# CAFA Agent Example: ASSISI Framework : On-the-fly Assessment Generation and Analysis

## 1\. Background: The Full 3-Phase ASSISI Framework

Need/Problem Statement: Traditional assessment methods often rely on static, pre-defined instruments (like surveys or quizzes with fixed items). This approach struggles with inflexibility, failing to adapt to specific user needs or emerging contexts. Furthermore, the analysis of results typically occurs only after data collection is finished, creating a significant delay between user interaction and actionable insights. This delay hinders real-time understanding and timely intervention. The ASSISI framework, particularly when augmented with dynamic item generation as demonstrated here, directly tackles these issues. It enables the creation of tailored assessment instruments on-the-fly and facilitates immediate, intelligent analysis upon completion, offering a more responsive and insightful approach.

This agent demonstrates the complete ASSISI (AI-Supported Survey Instrument and Simultaneous Investigator) framework, a powerful model designed for workflows requiring dynamic content generation followed by immediate analysis. It encompasses three distinct, sequential phases:

1. Phase 1: Generative Survey Instrument (Turns 1-3): This phase focuses on creating the assessment content dynamically. Instead of using a fixed set of questions, the agent leverages Automatic Item Generation (AIG).  
   * It begins by capturing the user's desired topic or context (Turn 1).  
   * An LLM, acting as an "assessment designer" (Turn 2), then generates a set of 5 unique assessment items specifically tailored to this context. This includes generating question stems, determining appropriate CAFA input command types (RADIO, TEXTAREA, etc.), crafting relevant options, and potentially defining correct answers.  
   * To ensure reliability, this generation process uses Structured Output (output-values) constrained by a predefined JSON schema (@J@). This forces the LLM's output into a consistent, machine-readable format.  
   * The generated JSON array of items is then stored using the @SETJ() command (Turn 3), making it available for the next phase.  
2. Phase 2: Administrative Survey Instrument (Turns 4-7): This phase focuses on presenting the dynamically generated assessment to the user and collecting their responses.  
   * A REPEAT loop (Turn 4\) manages the administration, iterating once for each generated item.  
   * Within the loop, symbolic logic first prepares the options for the current item (Turn 5), isolating them for reliable processing.  
   * The core of this phase is Turn 6, which dynamically displays the appropriate input control (e.g., RADIO, CHECKBOX) using command indirection (@@...). This technique allows the agent to call the specific CAFA command whose name was generated by the LLM in Phase 1\. The question stem and options (formatted using @JSONVALS()) are also populated dynamically from the stored JSON data.  
   * Finally, the user's response is captured using a similar indirection pattern (Turn 7\) and stored uniquely for each item.  
3. Phase 3: Simultaneous Investigator (Turn 8): This final phase performs the analysis once all data is collected.  
   * The last LLM turn acts as the "assessment analyst."  
   * It receives the *complete* context simultaneously: all the questions generated in Phase 1, and all the user answers collected in Phase 2, along with any correct answers defined during generation.  
   * The LLM synthesizes this comprehensive dataset to provide an immediate, holistic analysis or summary of the user's performance, delivering insights without the delay found in traditional methods.

This agent exemplifies a sophisticated workflow where AI plays multiple roles: content creator (Phase 1\) and analyst (Phase 3), bridged by efficient symbolic logic for dynamic administration (Phase 2). This creates a highly adaptive and context-aware assessment experience from start to finish.

Omit or leave as empty array [] for TEXTAREA, TEXT.>\"],\"correct_answer\":\"<string: Optional - The correct answer value, primarily used for cognitive assessments to enable grading>\"}]",
                "cond": "SELF",

            },
            "GENERATOR_PERSONA": {

Based on the user's provided context ('@TEXTAREA(user_context)@'), generate a short assessment with exactly 5 items covering key aspects of that topic. Use a variety of input controls (RADIO, CHECKBOX, TEXT, TEXTAREA, SELECT). For each item, provide: 'item_index', 'question_stem', the CAFA 'input_command' name (e.g., 'RADIO'), an 'option_list' (use empty array [] for TEXT/TEXTAREA), and optionally a 'correct_answer' if applicable for the topic and command type. Output ONLY the JSON matching the structure defined in Structured output.",
                "cond": "SELF",

            },
            "ANALYST_PERSONA": {
                "org": "You are an expert assessment analyst. Review the full list of questions, the user's corresponding answers, and the correct answers (if provided). Provide a concise, overall summary of the user's performance and understanding based on their responses across all items.",
                "cond": "SELF",
                "desc": "System prompt for the final analysis turn."
            }
        }
    },
    "prompts": [

## 3\. Detailed Code Explanation

### The options Object (Configuration)

This object holds the agent's metadata and predefined parameters that guide its behavior.

* J: Defines the required JSON structure (schema) for each assessment item generated by the LLM in Turn 2\. This schema dictates the keys (item\_index, question\_stem, input\_command, option\_list, correct\_answer) and expected data types, serving as the template for the output-values constraint.  
* GENERATOR\_PERSONA: Provides the detailed instructions (system prompt) for the LLM in Turn 2\. It specifies the role ("expert assessment designer"), the input context (@TEXTAREA(user\_context)@), the task requirements (generate 5 items, use varied controls), the specific data fields needed for each item, and critically, the constraint to output *only* JSON matching the defined schema (@J@).  
* ANALYST\_PERSONA: Contains the system prompt for the final LLM turn (Turn 8), instructing it to act as an "expert assessment analyst" and detailing the required analysis (review questions, user answers, correct answers, provide overall summary).

### The prompts Array (Turn-by-Turn Logic)

This array defines the agent's sequential execution flow, integrating the three ASSISI phases.

* Phase 1: Generative Survey Instrument (Turns 1-3)  
  * Turn 1 (Get Context \- Symbolic ⚙️): A straightforward turn using the @TEXTAREA() command to display a prompt and collect the user's desired assessment topic or context. The input is stored internally under the name user\_context.  
  * Turn 2 (Generate Items \- LLM 🤖 \- Hidden): The core Automatic Item Generation (AIG) step. This turn is hidden (show: false). It sends the GENERATOR\_PERSONA and the captured user\_context to the LLM. The output-values: "@J@" directive enforces the JSON schema, ensuring the LLM's response (stored in @TR2@) is a valid JSON array of 5 assessment items.  
  * Turn 3 (Store Items \- Symbolic ⚙️ \- Hidden): This turn processes the result from Turn 2\. It uses the @SETJ() command to parse the JSON string from @TR@TN(-1)@@ (which resolves to @TR2@) and store the resulting array of objects into the ITEMS JSON Parameter (JP). Note the adherence to the @SETJ() quoting exception (arguments are not double-quoted).  
* Phase 2: Administrative Survey Instrument (Turns 4-7)  
  * Turn 4 (Setup Loop \- Symbolic ⚙️ \- Hidden): Initiates the administration phase. The @REPEAT() command configures a loop to execute the next three turns (T5, T6, T7) exactly five times, corresponding to the five generated items.  
  * Turns 5-7 (The Assessment Loop \- Symbolic ⚙️): This block executes five times, with the @R\_i@ variable tracking the current iteration (1 through 5).  
    * Turn 5 (Prep Options \- Hidden): Prepares data for display. It accesses the ITEMS JP to get the option\_list array for the current item (@ITEMS\[@R\_i@\].option\_list@). It uses @SETJ() again to store this potentially nested array into a temporary CHOICES JP. This isolation simplifies the use of @JSONVALS() in the next turn.  
    * Turn 6 (Display Item \- Visible): Presents the current assessment item to the user. It uses command indirection (@@ITEMS\[@R\_i@\].input\_command@(...)) to dynamically invoke the correct CAFA input command (RADIO, CHECKBOX, etc.) based on the name stored in the ITEMS JSON. The command's arguments are filled dynamically: Q\_@R\_i@ creates a unique name for the input control for this iteration, @ITEMS\[@R\_i@\].question\_stem@ provides the question text, and @JSONVALS(CHOICES)@ extracts the options from the CHOICES JP and formats them into the pipe-separated string required by commands like RADIO or SELECT.  
    * Turn 7 (Capture Response \- Hidden): Records the user's input. It uses the same indirection pattern (@@ITEMS\[@R\_i@\].input\_command@(Q\_@R\_i@)@) to call the appropriate retrieval function for the input control displayed in Turn 6\. The captured answer is stored in a dynamically named parameter (e.g., USER\_ANS\_1, USER\_ANS\_2, etc.).  
* Phase 3: Simultaneous Investigator (Turn 8\)  
  * Turn 8 (Analyze Results \- LLM 🤖 \- Visible): This is the final analysis step. It activates the ANALYST\_PERSONA. The user prompt is carefully constructed to provide the LLM with all necessary information gathered throughout the agent's execution: it retrieves and labels the question stem, the user's captured answer (@USER\_ANS\_1@ to @USER\_ANS\_5@), and the correct answer (if provided in the JSON, e.g., @ITEMS\[1\].correct\_answer@) for *all five items*. This complete dataset is sent simultaneously, allowing the LLM to perform a holistic synthesis and generate the final summary report.

## 5\. Best Practices and Key Takeaways

* Full ASSISI Cycle: This agent successfully demonstrates the complete 3-phase ASSISI framework, showcasing the powerful synergy between AI-driven Generation of the instrument, rule-based Symbolic Administration, and insightful AI-driven Investigation. This highlights a shift from static surveys to dynamic, context-aware assessment processes, providing timely insights.  
* Structured Output Crucial for AIG: Employing output-values (Turn 2\) with a clearly defined JSON schema (@J@) is absolutely essential when using an LLM for Automatic Item Generation (AIG). It acts as a hard constraint, guaranteeing that the generated content (like assessment items with varying structures) adheres to a predictable format. This reliability is paramount for ensuring subsequent symbolic turns (SETJ, @ITEMS\[...\]@, JSONVALS) can correctly parse and utilize the data without errors that could derail the agent's workflow. Relying solely on prompt instructions for formatting is inherently less reliable and prone to inconsistencies, especially with complex outputs.  
* JP for Complex Data: JSON Parameters (ITEMS, CHOICES) are the appropriate tool for handling the inherently nested and structured nature of assessment items (which include stems, options, types, and answers). They provide a much cleaner and more intuitive way to manage this complexity compared to attempting to flatten the data into multiple parallel pipe-separated lists (AP). Remember the specific quoting exception for the @SETJ() command (arguments are *not* double-quoted) to avoid syntax errors when storing JSON strings dynamically during agent execution.  
* Dynamic UI with Indirection: Command indirection (@@...) is a cornerstone technique for building adaptive interfaces in CAFA. In this agent (Turn 6), @@ITEMS\[@R\_i@\].input\_command@(...) allows the user interface element itself (e.g., RADIO, CHECKBOX, TEXTAREA) to be determined dynamically based on the data generated by the LLM in Turn 2\. This enables the agent to present a varied assessment experience, mixing different question types within a single, efficient loop structure, rather than requiring separate logic branches for each input type.  
* JSONVALS Bridge: The @JSONVALS() command is the vital link enabling interoperability between complex JSON Parameters (JP) and the many CAFA symbolic commands designed to work with simpler pipe-separated lists (AP format). By extracting specific data (like the option texts) from a JP array (CHOICES in T5) and transforming it into the required format ("Option A|Option B|..."), @JSONVALS() allows commands like @RADIO() (in T6) to function correctly even when dealing with dynamically generated, structured data. The best practice of isolating the target array into its own JP (CHOICES) before applying @JSONVALS() enhances the command's reliability, especially when dealing with potentially nested or complex data structures within the original JSON.  
* Modularity: Adhering to a clear separation of concerns—distinct phases for generation, administration, and analysis—results in a more organized and robust agent. This modularity significantly simplifies debugging, as issues can often be localized to a specific phase or turn (e.g., problems with item generation vs. problems with response capture). It also makes the agent easier to maintain and adapt; for instance, the generation logic (T2) could be swapped out or refined (e.g., adding difficulty constraints) without affecting the administration loop (T4-T7) or the final analysis structure (T8).

## 6\. Possible Extensions

This foundational agent provides a robust starting point. It can be extended in numerous ways to create more sophisticated assessment tools and workflows:

* Add Symbolic Grading: Integrate immediate feedback and scorekeeping capabilities. This involves inserting a hidden symbolic turn *within* the REPEAT loop (e.g., after Turn 7, adjusting the loop end target in T4 accordingly). This new turn would check if the correct\_answer field exists and is non-empty for the current item (@ITEMS\[@R\_i@\].correct\_answer@). If a correct answer is available, it would use MAP or EVAL to compare the user's captured response (@USER\_ANS\_@R\_i@@) against it. For example, @EVAL("@USER\_ANS\_@R\_i@@ \== @ITEMS\[@R\_i@\].correct\_answer@")@ yields true/false. This boolean result can then update a running USER\_SCORE parameter using @SET(USER\_SCORE, "@EVAL('@USER\_SCORE@ \+ (@MAP(..., 'true', '1|0')@)')@")@. The final analysis in Turn 8 could then receive this calculated USER\_SCORE as additional context, enabling the AI analyst to provide quantitative feedback alongside qualitative insights. This adds an immediate layer of objective scoring to the assessment process.  
* Implement SCREAM Framework: Transition to a deeper diagnostic assessment model by incorporating the collection of user reasoning. This requires modifying the GENERATOR\_PERSONA (T2) to *exclusively* generate items where the input\_command is "RADIO". Furthermore, the generator must be instructed to include a relevant reasoning\_prompt string within each generated item's JSON (e.g., "reasoning\_prompt": "Explain the steps you took to arrive at this answer."). The JSON schema (J) would need to be updated to reflect this new field. In the administration phase, the display turn (T6) must be adapted to use the 4-argument version of the @RADIO() command: @RADIO(Q\_@R\_i@, "@ITEMS\[@R\_i@\].question\_stem@", "@JSONVALS(CHOICES)@", "@ITEMS\[@R\_i@\].reasoning\_prompt@")@. This setup captures both the selected option (SR) and the user's written explanation (CR) together, storing them typically as "SR|CR" in the USER\_ANS\_@R\_i@ parameter. Finally, the ANALYST\_PERSONA (T8) needs significant enhancement. It must be instructed to parse the SR and CR components (e.g., using @USER\_ANS\_@R\_i@\[1\]@ and @USER\_ANS\_@R\_i@\[2\]@) and explicitly compare them, looking for alignment, contradictions, or specific types of misconceptions revealed in the reasoning. This elevates the analysis from simple performance summary to a nuanced diagnosis of the user's thought process.  
* Refine Generator Quality: Enhance the control over the dynamically generated items to improve their precision and pedagogical value. This involves adding more specific constraints, instructions, or guiding examples within the GENERATOR\_PERSONA prompt (T2). For example, you could instruct the LLM to target items towards a particular cognitive level based on Bloom's Taxonomy (e.g., "Generate items assessing 'Analysis' or 'Evaluation' level understanding of the topic"). You might specify desired difficulty parameters (e.g., "Generate 2 easy, 2 medium, and 1 hard item"). Additionally, providing negative constraints (e.g., "Avoid negatively phrased question stems," "Ensure distractors are plausible but clearly incorrect") or including a few high-quality example items directly within the prompt can significantly steer the LLM towards producing better, more consistent, and instructionally sound outputs. This allows for much finer-grained control over the assessment's characteristics.  
* Error Handling for Generation: Increase the agent's resilience by adding validation steps for the LLM's generated content before attempting to use it. Insert a new hidden symbolic turn immediately after the generation turn (Turn 2). This new turn (e.g., Turn 2.5) would use EVAL or potentially string manipulation commands (like checking character counts or presence of specific substrings) to perform basic structural checks on the generated JSON string (@TR2@). For example, it could verify if the string starts with \[ and ends with \], or count the occurrences of key elements like "question\_stem": to estimate if 5 items were generated. If this validation logic detects a potential issue (e.g., @EVAL("...")@ returns false), a MAP and JUMP command within the same turn could redirect the agent's flow to a dedicated error-handling turn. This error turn could inform the user about the generation issue and potentially offer options like retrying the generation (jumping back to T2) or exiting gracefully, thus preventing the agent from crashing later during parsing (T3) due to malformed input.  
* Save/Load Assessments (Persistence & Reusability): Enable the capability to save generated assessment instances for later use or sharing. After successfully generating and storing the items in the ITEMS JP (Turn 3), add another hidden symbolic turn (e.g., Turn 3.5). In this turn, use the @EXPORT("ITEMS", "assessment\_@TEXT(user\_topic\_context)@")@ command. This bundles the entire ITEMS JSON structure into a portable package and saves it to a unique Data ID (DID). Using the original topic (@TEXT(user\_topic\_context)@) within the DID name makes it easier to identify later. This saved assessment package could then be loaded by a different CAFA agent, or later in the same agent during a different session, using the @IMPORT("assessment\_...")@ command. This effectively allows for the creation, archival, sharing, and re-administration of specific, dynamically generated assessment instances, moving beyond the limitation of single-session use and enabling longitudinal studies or standardized comparisons using tailored instruments.

# CAFA Agent Example: Between-Task GAMER with Human Curator

## 1\. Background: Between-Task GAMER and Human Curation

This agent demonstrates a powerful "Between-Task GAMER" framework, a form of simple reinforcement learning driven by human feedback (RLHF). Unlike a standard GAMER model that refines a single output *within* one session (Generation \-\> Reflection \-\> Evolution), this agent applies the cycle *across* multiple user sessions or tasks. The human user acts as the crucial "Curator" or "Critic" in this loop.

1. Generation (State Across Tasks): The agent starts by loading its cumulative history (the LOG), which represents its current learned state or "draft" understanding based on all past interactions. It then generates an output for the user's current request, using this historical context.  
2. Reflection (Human Curation): After seeing the generated output, the user provides feedback. They classify the output as a "Good Example" or "Bad Example" and, importantly, provide a textual rationale explaining *why*. This curated feedback is the core "reflection" step, providing qualitative insight into the agent's performance. The user also has the option to simply end the session without providing feedback.  
3. Evolution (Knowledge Update): If feedback is given, the agent structures the original input, the generated output, the classification (Good/Bad), and the user's rationale into a Markdown-formatted entry. This entry is appended to the persistent LOG. This updated LOG represents the "evolved" knowledge base, ready to inform the "Generation" step for the *next* user or task, thus closing the reinforcement learning loop.

This cycle allows the agent's performance to iteratively improve over time, guided directly by human judgment and explanation, using the persistent LOG as its evolving memory.

## 2\. Full Agent Code

Analyze the 'Input', 'Output', 'Classification' ('Good Example'/'Bad Example'), and 'Rationale of Good/Bad' within each entry. Aim to produce outputs similar to 'Good' examples and avoid patterns from 'Bad' examples.",

## 3\. Detailed Code Explanation

### The options Object (Configuration)

* MARKDOWN\_GENERATOR\_PERSONA: Defines the instructions for the core generation LLM (Turn 3). It explicitly tells the AI to use the historical Markdown entries (provided via the FullLog parameter) to guide its output, paying attention to the Input, Output, Classification, and Rationale of Good/Bad fields within those entries.

### The prompts Array (Turn-by-Turn Logic)

1. T1 (Load Log \- Symbolic ⚙️ \- Hidden): Loads the entire raw Markdown log history from persistent storage (LOG) into the FullLog parameter. This represents the current state of learned knowledge.  
2. T2 (Get User Input \- Symbolic ⚙️ \- Visible): Prompts the current user for their input/request using @TEXTAREA().  
3. T3 (Generate Output \- LLM 🤖 \- Visible):  
   * Generation Step: The core generation happens here.  
   * System Prompt: Provides the MARKDOWN\_GENERATOR\_PERSONA instructions *and* the entire raw @FullLog@ history to the LLM.  
   * User Prompt: Provides the current UserInput.  
   * The LLM generates an output informed by both the current request and the curated examples from the past. Temperature is lowered slightly (0.1) to encourage more adherence to the examples.  
4. T4 (Store Output \- Symbolic ⚙️ \- Hidden): Saves the generated output (@TR3@) into the GeneratedOutput parameter.  
5. T5 (Display for Curation \- Symbolic ⚙️ \- Visible): Presents the UserInput and GeneratedOutput clearly to the user (the Curator) for review.  
6. T6 (Capture Curator Action \- Symbolic ⚙️ \- Visible):  
   * Reflection Step (Start): Asks the Curator to classify the output using @RADIO() with options "Good Example," "Bad Example," or "End Session."  
7. T7 (Router \- Symbolic ⚙️ \- Hidden): Checks the Curator's choice. If "End Session," it jumps directly to the END turn (T12). Otherwise, continues to collect the rationale.  
8. T8 (Ask for Curator Rationale \- Symbolic ⚙️ \- Visible):  
   * Reflection Step (Detail): If feedback is being given, prompts the Curator to explain their reasoning using @TEXTAREA().  
9. T9 (Create Markdown Entry \- Symbolic ⚙️ \- Hidden):  
   * Evolution Step (Prepare): Constructs the structured Markdown string for the log entry. It includes the UserInput, GeneratedOutput, the classification ("Good Example" or "Bad Example"), the FeedbackRationale, and a timestamp.  
10. T10 (Save Log Entry \- Symbolic ⚙️ \- Hidden):  
    * Evolution Step (Commit): Appends the NewLogEntryMarkdown string to the persistent LOG using @SAVE() with the true flag. This updates the agent's knowledge base for future runs.  
11. T11 (Confirmation \- Symbolic ⚙️ \- Visible): Informs the user that their feedback has been saved.  
12. T12 (End Turn \- Symbolic ⚙️ \- Hidden): Contains the @END@ command to terminate the session if requested.

## 5\. Best Practices and Key Takeaways

* Human-in-the-Loop Learning: This agent operationalizes RLHF by integrating the human user as a curator directly into the learning loop. The quality of the curated feedback (classification \+ rationale) directly influences future performance.  
* Between-Task GAMER: Demonstrates how the GAMER cycle can be applied *across* sessions, using the LOG as the persistent medium for passing the "evolved" state from one task/user to the next.  
* Log as Evolving Knowledge Base: The persistent LOG becomes more than just a record; it acts as the agent's memory and evolving understanding of good vs. bad outputs for given inputs.  
* Markdown for Readability & Structure: Using Markdown strikes a balance. It's human-readable, allowing curators or developers to easily inspect the log, while still providing enough structure (headings, code blocks) for the LLM to parse (with appropriate prompting).  
* Importance of Rationale: Collecting the *why* behind the classification provides much richer signal for the LLM to learn from compared to just a binary Good/Bad label.

## 6\. Possible Extensions

* Curator Review Interface: Instead of appending directly, save feedback to a temporary "pending" log. A separate "Reviewer" agent could then load this pending log, allow a senior curator to review/edit/approve entries, and only then append approved entries to the main LOG.  
* Sampling Strategy: If the log becomes very large, modify Turn 1 or add a new turn to implement a sampling strategy (e.g., load only the most recent N entries, or a random sample) to keep the generation prompt (T3) manageable.  
* More Granular Feedback: Change the @RADIO() in T6 to allow for more nuanced ratings (e.g., a 1-5 scale) and update the logging and persona accordingly.  
* JSON Logging: Switch back to JSON logging (using @SETJ() and @SAVE()) if machine-readability and parsing robustness become more critical than human readability, especially if the log data needs to be consumed by other automated systems.

## References

* Choi, J. (2025). CAFA Agent Example: Between-Task GAMER with Human Curator. In *Collective AI on the Foundation AI (CAFA): The pathway of digital transformation of intelligence*. CAFA Lab, Inc.

# CAFA Agent Example: Simple AoA Workflow using MACRO Essential

## 1\. Background: Orchestrating Agent Collaboration for Assessment on the AI

This example demonstrates a foundational concept in advanced CAFA development: using agent-to-agent interaction to build complex workflows. We'll create a simple pipeline where multiple specialized agents collaborate by triggering each other and passing data. While the mechanism involves agent-on-agent communication, the specific agents in this example—ALPHA, GARAM, and GRADE—are named in the context of Assessment on the AI (AoA), showcasing how this pattern can automate assessment-related tasks.

The key enabling technology is the CAFA MACRO (Multi-Agent Context Routing and Orchestration) Essential standard. MACRO provides a standardized way for one agent (the *caller*) to invoke another agent (the *callee* or *target*) and pass it an initial piece of data using a URL parameter named ID\_ID (Input Data ID). The target agent is designed to detect this ID\_ID and automatically execute a specific "MACRO Path" using the provided data, bypassing the need for initial user interaction.

We will implement the conceptual workflow:

1. ALPHA (AI-based Lesson Plan for Harmonic Assessment): Generates a lesson plan based on user input, saves it, and provides a link to trigger GARAM, passing the lesson plan's Data ID (DID).  
2. GARAM (Generative Assessment Rubric by AI Model): Receives the lesson plan DID via ID\_ID, loads the plan, generates a corresponding rubric, saves it, and provides a link to trigger GRADE, passing the rubric's DID.  
3. GRADE (Generative Review by AI for Developmental Evaluation): Receives the rubric DID via ID\_ID, loads the rubric, prompts the user for an essay, and scores it using the loaded rubric.

This chain showcases how specialized agents can be linked seamlessly using the MACRO Essential protocol to automate a multi-step assessment creation process.

## 2\. Development Process: Target First, Caller Later

Developing a MACRO-based workflow requires a specific order: build and save the target agent *before* finalizing the calling agent. This is because the calling agent needs the target agent's unique Agent ID to construct the correct invocation URL.

Steps:

1. Develop GRADE (Final Target) First:  
   * Implement the Turn 1 Router (@JUMP(@MAP(...))@ checking ID\_ID).  
   * Implement its fully automatic MACRO Path (load rubric) which then converges with the Interactive Path to ask for the essay and perform scoring.  
   * Implement the Interactive Path (ask for rubric manually) which also converges to the essay prompt and scoring.  
   * Save GRADE and note its Agent ID.  
2. Develop GARAM (Middle Agent) Next:  
   * Implement its fully automatic MACRO Path (load plan, generate rubric, save rubric to OD\_ID).  
   * Implement the Final Handoff Turn with the MACRO link to GRADE, using GRADE's actual Agent ID.  
   * Save GARAM and note its Agent ID.  
3. Develop ALPHA (Initial Caller) Last:  
   * Implement its core interactive logic to gather inputs and generate the plan.  
   * Implement the Final Handoff Turn with the MACRO link to GARAM, using GARAM's actual Agent ID.  
   * Save ALPHA.

#### Code Explanation (GRADE) \- Updated for Revised Code

* options.params: Includes ID\_ID (standard MACRO input), LOADED\_RUBRIC (to hold the rubric), and TEMP\_RUBRIC\_DATA (used for the LOAD separation rule).  
* T1 (Router): Standard MACRO router checking ID\_ID. Jumps to T2 (Interactive) if empty, or T5 (MACRO) if present.  
* T2-T4 (Interactive Path):  
  * T2: Uses @TEXTAREA("rubric\_input", ...) to display a prompt and wait for the user to paste the rubric.  
  * T3: Hidden turn captures the user's input using @TEXTAREA(rubric\_input) and saves it into LOADED\_RUBRIC using @SET.  
  * T4: Hidden turn uses @JUMP to skip the MACRO Path steps (T5, T6, T7) and go directly to the common "Ask for Essay" logic starting at T8.  
* T5-T7 (MACRO Path):  
  * T5: Hidden symbolic turn indicating the MACRO Path.  
  * T6: Hidden turn uses @LOAD(@ID\_ID@)@ to retrieve the rubric via DID and stores it *temporarily* in TEMP\_RUBRIC\_DATA. This adheres to the rule of separating LOAD from its usage.  
  * T7: Hidden turn copies the data from TEMP\_RUBRIC\_DATA into the main LOADED\_RUBRIC parameter.  
* T8-T9 (Common Scoring Logic): Both paths converge here.  
  * T8: Visible symbolic turn uses @TEXTAREA("essay\_input", ...) to confirm the rubric is loaded and prompts the user to paste the essay, waiting for input.  
  * T9: Visible LLM turn performs scoring. It receives LOADED\_RUBRIC and the essay text entered by the user (@TEXTAREA(essay\_input)). The LLM provides the score and justification. The agent ends.

## 7\. Tips for MACRO Workflow Development

* Target First, Caller Later: This remains the cardinal rule. You absolutely must build, save, and retrieve the unique Agent ID of the *receiving* (target) agent (like GRADE) *before* you can finalize the code of the *calling* agent (like GARAM) that needs to construct the invocation URL. Attempting to build in sequence without the target's ID will lead to non-functional links.  
* Incremental Development: Build complex workflows piece by piece. Start by creating the simplest possible versions of each agent (perhaps just passing a fixed "Hello World" message via ID\_ID). Focus intently on getting the MACRO handoffs (the @SAVE(), OD\_ID, URL construction, Turn 1 router, and @LOAD()) working flawlessly between agents *first*. Once the basic pipeline is confirmed to function correctly, *then* go back and enhance the internal logic of each agent (e.g., upgrading a simple LLM call to a more sophisticated GAMER or RISE framework). This isolates potential issues, making debugging significantly easier.  
* Use Parameters for Agent IDs: Hardcoding Agent IDs directly into the handoff URL within a turn's user prompt is functional but brittle. A much better practice is to store the target Agent ID in an Agent Parameter within the options.params object (e.g., NEXT\_AGENT\_ID). Then, construct the handoff URL dynamically using this parameter: .../@NEXT\_AGENT\_ID@/ID\_ID=@OD\_ID@. This centralizes the configuration. If the target agent's ID ever changes (e.g., you save a new version), you only need to update the NEXT\_AGENT\_ID parameter in the calling agent, rather than hunting down and editing the URL string within the prompts array.  
* Test Each Link in Isolation: After building a connection (e.g., ALPHA \-\> GARAM), test *only that specific link*. Run the calling agent (ALPHA), click the generated MACRO link, and meticulously verify that the target agent (GARAM) launches correctly *and* successfully executes its MACRO Path (e.g., check that it loaded the data passed via ID\_ID). Fix any issues with this single link before proceeding to build the next connection (e.g., GARAM \-\> GRADE). Isolating tests prevents compounding errors.  
* Thoroughly Check ID\_ID Handling: Double-check the logic in the target agent. Verify that its Turn 1 router uses the correct syntax (@JUMP(@MAP("@ID\_ID@", "", "@TN(Interactive)@|@TN(MACRO)@")@)@) to detect the presence or absence of the ID\_ID. Critically, ensure that the very first operational step within the MACRO Path (the turn immediately following the router jump) is the @LOAD(@ID\_ID@)@ command to retrieve the data passed from the caller. Forgetting this LOAD step is a common error.  
* Verify @SAVE() and OD\_ID Usage: In the calling agent, confirm that the turn responsible for generating the output data is followed by a turn that correctly uses @SAVE() to persist that data. Ensure the result of the @SAVE() command (the new Data ID) is captured into a parameter, conventionally named OD\_ID. Finally, verify that this @OD\_ID@ parameter is correctly referenced within the MACRO handoff URL constructed in the final turn (.../ID\_ID=@OD\_ID@). Any mistake in this save-capture-link sequence will break the data flow.

## 8\. Future Work

This simple AoA workflow provides a solid foundation. Its modular design allows for significant enhancements and adaptations:

* Enhance Agent Logic (Incremental Approach): The current agents employ straightforward LLM calls. A recommended next step, following the principle of incremental development, is to enhance these *after* confirming the basic MACRO connections function reliably. Start simple: ensure ALPHA passes data to GARAM, and GARAM passes data to GRADE using the existing basic LLM turns. Once this core MACRO pipeline is stable, you can then begin upgrading the internal logic. For instance, ALPHA's lesson plan generation could be evolved to use the GAMER framework, adding turns for critique and refinement *within* ALPHA, while still maintaining the same final @SAVE() and handoff turn structure required by GARAM. Similarly, GARAM's rubric generation could be expanded into a GAMER loop *after* the initial @LOAD() step, producing a more robust rubric before the final @SAVE() and handoff. GRADE's scoring logic could eventually incorporate the RISE framework *after* loading the rubric and receiving the essay, adding iterative self-critique to its scoring process. This methodical, step-by-step enhancement ensures the critical MACRO compliance is maintained throughout development, making the system more robust and easier to debug as complexity increases.  
* Pass Multiple Parameters: The current MACRO Essential standard supports passing only a single ID\_ID. Future iterations of the MACRO standard could potentially allow passing multiple distinct Data IDs or even key-value pairs via URL parameters (e.g., .../RubricDID=XXX\&EssayDID=YYY). This would enable richer context handoffs, allowing GRADE, for example, to receive both the rubric *and* a previously saved student essay simultaneously, further automating the workflow. This capability would significantly expand the possibilities for complex inter-agent collaboration.  
* Implement Robust Error Handling: The current agents assume the workflow proceeds smoothly and without issue. To make the system more resilient, add conditional logic using MAP and JUMP to gracefully handle potential failures. For example, if @LOAD(@ID\_ID@)@ in GARAM or GRADE fails (perhaps due to an invalid DID being passed, or the data being inaccessible), the agent could detect the failure (e.g., the loaded parameter remains empty or contains an error marker) and jump to a specific error-handling turn. This turn could inform the user that the necessary data couldn't be retrieved and perhaps suggest alternative actions, like attempting the step manually, rather than simply failing silently or proceeding with corrupted data. Similarly, basic checks could be added after LLM generation turns (e.g., checking if the result @TR@TN(-1)@@ is empty or contains error indicators) before attempting to save or use the generated content.  
* Incorporate User Choice and Branching: Modify the handoff turns to provide the user with more agency and control over the workflow. Instead of automatically proceeding to the next agent, ALPHA's final turn (T5) could be enhanced to present RADIO buttons or clickable links offering choices like "\[Generate Rubric Automatically (GARAM)\]" versus "\[Enter Rubric Manually\]". Based on the user's selection, a subsequent hidden symbolic turn using MAP and JUMP could either trigger the standard MACRO link to GARAM *or* route the user to a different sequence of turns within ALPHA (or potentially invoke a different, simpler agent) designed specifically for manual rubric input. This transforms the rigid pipeline into a more flexible, user-directed process, accommodating different user preferences or scenarios where automated generation might not be desired or appropriate.

## 9\. Agent Import Instructions

You can import the code for each agent into the CAFA platform by following these steps:

1. Click the copy button located at the top-right of the JSON code block for the agent you wish to import (GRADE, GARAM, or ALPHA).  
2. Go to https://ai.cafalab.com/.  
3. Click 'Create Agent'.  
4. Select 'Build from Scratch'.  
5. Click 'Import from Text'.  
6. Paste the copied code into the text field.  
7. Click 'Import'.  
8. Save the agent and note down the Agent ID. This ID is crucial for configuring the NEXT\_AGENT\_ID parameter in the subsequent agents (e.g., the ID for GRADE must be placed into GARAM, and the ID for GARAM must be placed into ALPHA).

# CAFA Agent Example: OMG \- Dynamic Format Quiz

## 1\. Background: Dynamic Command Execution and User Choice

OMG (Ontology Model-centered Generation) is a key theoretical framework within CAFA, focusing on using structured knowledge to drive agent behavior. This agent exemplifies OMG by employing a pre-defined ontology model—specifically, a tabular representation storing pairs of statistical terms (Answer\_Feature) and their descriptions (Stem\_Feature)—to generate diverse quiz items. Furthermore, it showcases a sophisticated technique: dynamic command execution. Instead of using a fixed input control (like @RADIO()@), the agent empowers the user to select their preferred quiz format (e.g., Radio Buttons, Text Area). It then dynamically invokes the corresponding CAFA command based on the user's choice, demonstrating how OMG principles can enable flexible and user-adaptive interfaces.

Key Concepts Illustrated:

* Ontology Model (SHUFFLE/LINK): The core quiz content resides in linked parameters (Stem\_Feature, Answer\_Feature). SHUFFLE randomizes the item order, while LINK ensures the correct term-description pairs are maintained, demonstrating a simple tabular ontology.  
* User Configuration: The agent starts by prompting the user to select their desired quiz item format from a predefined list (Format\_Choice).  
* Mapping Choice to Command: It translates the user's selection into an internal command name using INDEX to look up the choice in Format\_Choice and retrieve the corresponding command from the parallel Control list.  
* Dynamic Command Call (@@...): Central to the agent's flexibility, the double-at syntax (@@Selected\_Format@(...)) executes the command whose name was determined by the user's choice. This allows the same turn logic (Turn 4\) to render different UI controls (RADIO, TEXTAREA, etc.).  
* Looping (REPEAT/@R\_i@): The @REPEAT command iterates through the items defined in the ontology, using @R\_i@ to access the correctly linked data for each question.

This agent highlights how OMG, combined with dynamic command execution and user configuration, allows for the creation of adaptable applications orchestrated entirely through CAFA's symbolic commands and parameter system.

## 2\. Full Agent Code

## 3\. Detailed Code Explanation

### The options Object

This section defines the agent's metadata and its core knowledge base (Ontology Model) using Agent Parameters (params).

* Stem\_Feature: Contains the descriptions of statistical terms. cond: "SHUFFLE" ensures these are presented in a random order each time the agent runs.  
* Answer\_Feature: Contains the corresponding statistical terms (Mean, Median, etc.). cond: "LINK(Stem\_Feature)" is crucial; it forces this list to shuffle in the exact same order as Stem\_Feature, maintaining the correct description-term pairs.  
* Control: Stores the internal CAFA command names (TEXTAREA, RADIO, CHECKBOX) that correspond to the user's format choices. cond: "SELF" keeps them in a fixed order.  
* TOTAL\_ITEMS: Defines the number of items in the quiz (5).  
* Control\_Text: Contains the instructional text displayed before each question (e.g., "Select the best term..."). It's linked to Control to align with the chosen format, though linking to Stem\_Feature might be more semantically correct if the instruction varies per *item* rather than per *format*. *(Self-correction: The original code links to Control. This works if the command list and format choice list are parallel. Linking to Stem\_Feature would ensure it matches the shuffled item order directly).*  
* R\_Ext\_Text: Stores the text for the optional 4th argument of the RADIO command (used for explanations in the "SR+CR" format). Also linked.  
* Format\_Choice: Stores the user-facing names for the format options (e.g., "Constructed Response (CR)"). cond: "SELF" keeps them fixed.

### The prompts Array (Turn-by-Turn Logic)

* Turn 1 (Format Selection \- Symbolic ⚙️ \- Visible):  
  * Uses the @RADIO() command to present the user with the format choices defined in @Format\_Choice\[2:5\]@. The agent pauses here for user input.  
  * *Note: Removed model and output-values. Kept show: true as it's user-facing.*  
* Turn 2 (Map Choice to Command \- Symbolic ⚙️ \- Hidden):  
  * This turn determines which internal command to use.  
  * @RADIO(format\_selection)@: Retrieves the user's selected format name (e.g., "Selected Response(SR)").  
  * @INDEX("@Format\_Choice\[2:5\]@", ...): Finds the 1-based index (position) of the user's choice within the list of format names.  
  * @CONTROL\[...\]@: Uses the found index to retrieve the corresponding CAFA command name from the Control list (e.g., if "Selected Response(SR)" is the 2nd option, and the 2nd item in Control is "RADIO", it retrieves "RADIO").  
  * @SET(Selected\_Format, ...): Stores the retrieved command name (e.g., "RADIO") in the Selected\_Format parameter.  
  * *Note: Removed model and output-values. Set show: false explicitly.*  
* Turn 3 (Loop Setup \- Symbolic ⚙️ \- Hidden):  
  * Uses @REPEAT(@TN(1)@, @TN(1)@, @TOTAL\_ITEMS@) to set up a loop. It instructs the agent to execute the *next* turn (Turn 4\) exactly @TOTAL\_ITEMS@ (5) times.  
  * *Note: Removed model and output-values. Set show: false explicitly.*  
* Turn 4 (Dynamic Question Display \- Symbolic ⚙️ \- Visible \- Inside Loop):  
  * This is the core turn that runs 5 times.  
  * @@Selected\_Format@(...): This is the dynamic command call. The double-at @@ tells the CAFA system to first resolve the value of Selected\_Format (e.g., "RADIO") and then execute *that command*.  
  * The arguments for the dynamic command are constructed using @R\_i@ (the current loop iteration number) to fetch the correct Stem\_Feature, Answer\_Feature, Control\_Text, and R\_Ext\_Text for the current item.  
  * The agent pauses here in each iteration for the user's answer via the dynamically chosen input control.  
  * *Note: Removed model and output-values. Kept show: true and markdown: true.*  
* Turn 5 (Results Summary \- Symbolic ⚙️ \- Visible):  
  * Executes *after* the loop finishes.  
  * Displays a summary using Markdown (markdown: true).  
  * @@Selected\_Format@(Q\_1)@, @@Selected\_Format@(Q\_2)@, etc.: It again uses the dynamic command retrieval syntax (@@...) to call the appropriate retrieval function (e.g., @RADIO(Q\_1)@, @TEXTAREA(Q\_1)@) for each question number (1 through 5\) to display the user's previously submitted answers.  
  * *Note: Removed model and output-values. Kept show: true and markdown: true.*
